1.1: 1.1 The beginning of the Gospel. ISID. Gospel, good announcement, which properly pertains to the kingdom of God and the remission of sins. Hence: Do penance and believe the Gospel: and the kingdom of heaven is at hand. HIER. The four Gospels are one, and the one is four. Therefore the book of Mark is called a Gospel, and likewise those of the others: because all are one, and one is all. Of Jesus Christ. HIER. Jesus in Hebrew, Soter in Greek, Savior in Latin; Christ in Greek, Messias in Hebrew, anointed in Latin, that is, king and priest: he is said to be of the line of King David, and of Levi. The Son of God. BEDA. Matthew says: son of David, son of Abraham Matth. 1.. Mark says: Son of God, so that gradually from the lesser to the greater, etc., up to: John begins from the eternity of the Word of God, and ends in the resurrection of the Lord.
1.2: 1.2 As it is written. Mark puts first the testimonies of the prophets, by which he asserts that these things are not new but old, foreknown and foretold by the prophets, in which he both invites the Jews who had received the law and the prophets to the Gospel, and summons the Gentiles who held the Gospel to reverence for the law and the prophets, so that no one, like the heretics, may accept one without the other. Behold I send. BEDA. John is called an angel not by community of nature, as Origen falsely says, but by dignity of office: as also the priests, of whom it is said: The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the law at his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts Mal. 2.. THE SAME. Note that this testimony: Behold I send my angel, etc., is Malachi's, yet he says that both are Isaiah's, because, etc., up to: all the prophets spoke by one spirit as with one mouth.
1.3: 1.3 Of one crying. ISID. To the Jews, deaf, placed far off because of their sins, worthy of the cry of indignation. In the desert. In the desert the voice and cry are made: because Judea is a desert house, empty, swept, without the Spirit of God, prophet, king, priest. Hence Jesus and John seek what was lost in the desert. Where the devil conquered, there he is conquered: where man fell, there he rises. Prepare ye. ISID. Do penance and preach. Hence the Parasceve before the sabbath, etc., up to: that we may possess in quiet the desirable land. The way of the Lord. HIER. The way of the Lord by which he enters among men is penance, through which God descends to us and we ascend to him. Hence angels are recorded ascending and descending upon the Son of man. Make straight his paths. ISID. He commands that, going by the king's highway, we love our neighbors as ourselves, and we, etc., up to: that the mouth be not separated from the work, nor the work from the mouth. The paths come after the way, because the moral commandments are explained after penance according to Mark or Matthew. The way is prepared through faith and baptism and penance. The paths are made straight through the austere signs of garment, girdle, food, drink, and a very humble voice.
1.4: 1.4 John. ISID. Grace of God. He begins from the grace of God, hence follows: Baptizing, etc. By baptism sins are forgiven; hence: Freely have you received, freely give Matth. 10.. And the Apostle: By grace you are saved Ephes. 2.. Baptizing. HIER. He gave the baptism of penance, he preached baptism for the remission of sins, yet did not give it. As by preaching, etc., up to: now through the friend of the bridegroom the bride is led in, as Rebecca to Isaac, veiled by the servant with a white mantle.
1.5: 1.5 In the Jordan. THE SAME. Jordan, a foreign descent, where sins are absolved. For the ark, etc., up to: the body of Christ, to the unclean it does not profit, but changes to the worse. Confessing, etc. THE SAME. Confession and beauty are before his sight Psal. 115., that is, the bridegroom's. Hence the bride leaps down from the camel when the Church humbles herself to Christ, who is figured by Isaac, at whose birth God made laughter for Sara. As it is said to Mary, who is a princess with God: Blessed art thou among women Luc. 1.. BEDA. Confessing their sins they are baptized. For those who receive baptism ought to promise the newness of a better life, etc., up to: and so change those cleansed, professing the Christian religion, into members of the Church.
1.6: 1.6 And John was, etc. HIER. The garment of the prophet, and his food and drink, signify the whole austere life of those who preach, and the Gentiles, etc., up to: because all things are from the grace of the Gospel, in which there is no distinction of Jew and Greek. BEDA. Clothed with camel's hair. Because he did not foster sins but sharply rebuked, saying: Brood of vipers, etc. A leathern girdle, etc., up to: for in honey is sweetness, in the locust a lively flight, but quickly falling.
1.7: 1.7 One mightier than I. HIER. Who is mightier than the grace by which sins are washed away? He who, etc., up to: and reaches a hundred and forty-four thousand. To loose the latchet. BEDA. It was the custom among the ancients that if a man was unwilling to take as wife the woman who was fitting for him, he, etc., up to: I am not able to bare the footsteps of the Redeemer, because I do not usurp the name of bridegroom. HIER. The latchet of the shoes, that is, the mystery of the Incarnation of God. For the sole, etc., up to: the bride in the patriarchs, the friend in the prophets, the neighbor in Mary and Joseph, the beloved in John the Baptist, the dove in Christ and the apostles.
1.8: 1.8 I have baptized you with water. BEDA. John does not yet say openly that he is God or the Son of God, because his hearers were unlearned: but little by little through the glorified humanity he leads them to faith in the divinity, saying: He shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit. But afterward, when he saw them more capable, he now openly preaches the Son of God, saying: He gave testimony that this is the Son of God Joan. 3.. ISID. I baptize you with water, he, etc. The river of God always full, always equal, of which: The stream of the river maketh the city of God joyful Psal. 45.. Much differs, etc., up to: the anointing of Christ from the bitterness of the passion came to the glory of the resurrection; hence the Apostle: Have this mind in you, which was also in Christ Jesus, etc., up to: Wherefore God also hath exalted him Phil. 2..
1.9: 1.9 And he was baptized in the Jordan. For three reasons: to fulfill justice and humility; to approve the baptism of John; and, sanctifying the waters of the Jordan, to show by the descent of the dove that the Holy Spirit is present in baptism. HIER. Mark: As the hart desiring the fountains of water leaps, crops the heights of the meadows, bears palms on its head, like the honey-making bee tastes lightly the flowers of the field (whose fragrance is likened to the true Isaac). Hence Jesus coming from Nazareth of Galilee to baptism, etc., up to: To him that overcometh I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God Apoc. 2..
1.10: 1.10 He saw the heavens opened, etc. BEDA. The mystery of the Trinity is shown in baptism: the Son is baptized, the Spirit is in the dove, the Father sounds in the voice. The heavens are opened, etc., up to: will remain with us and be in us according to the measure of faith the Spirit. But of Christ it is said: Full of grace and truth Joan. 1.. Remaining on him. The Spirit remains in him, not from the time he was baptized, but from the time he was conceived. But that he descended in baptism signifies to us that spiritual grace is given in baptism, to those regenerated of water and the Spirit for the remission of sins, upon whom a fuller grace of the Spirit is wont to be given from heaven through the laying on of the bishop's hand.
1.11: 1.11 Thou art my beloved Son. BEDA. It is not that he is taught what he did not know, but what we ought to believe is shown to us, namely that he himself, etc., up to: and well does the Spirit descend in the form of a dove, a simple animal and without gall: because he seeks the simple, nor does he dwell in impure minds.
1.12: 1.12 The Spirit. THE SAME. Lest anyone doubt which spirit, Luke deliberately puts first: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan; then he continued: and was led by the Spirit into the desert, lest it be thought that an unclean spirit could do anything against him.
1.13: 1.13 Forty days. THE SAME. It signifies the whole time in which the devil tempts his members. For the world, fourfold, serves the Lord by observing the ten commandments, fighting against the devil. Four times ten make forty. Everywhere and always the adversary is present, who does not cease to hinder our journey. And he was with beasts. We too, if in the wilderness of holy conversation we tolerate with undefiled mind the beastly ways of men, deserve the mystery of angels, by whom, released from the body, we shall be carried into heaven.
1.14: 1.14 Now after that. ISID. We have received grace for grace, carnal things are beheaded, spiritual things are given life. The shadow ceasing, the truth is present. John in prison, the law in Judea, Jesus in Galilee, salvation among the Gentiles. Preaching, etc. HIER. Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom Matth. 5., etc. To an earthly kingdom poverty succeeds, to the poverty of Christians the everlasting kingdom; hence: My kingdom is not of this world Joan. 18.: for all earthly honor is foam, smoke, a dream.
1.15: 1.15 Do penance. HIER. The sweetness of the fruit repays the bitterness of the root: the hope of harbor delights amid the dangers of the sea, the hope of health mitigates the pain of medicine. He who desires the kernel, let him break the nut: let him do penance, who wishes to cling to the eternal good. Those can tell the praises of Christ who have deserved to reach the palm of forgiveness. Hence after penance preachers are chosen.
1.16: 1.16 He saw Simon. HIER. Simon, obedient; Andrew, manly; James, supplanter; John, grace. By these names, etc., up to: through prudence we obey, through justice we act manfully, through temperance we trample serpents, through fortitude we merit the grace of God. THE SAME. Whom does secular eloquence not intoxicate? It is difficult for powerful men, and nobles, and rich men, and much more difficult for the eloquent to believe in God. Their mind is blinded by riches and wealth and luxury, and, surrounded by vices, they cannot see virtues, and they judge the simplicity of holy Scripture not by the majesty of its meanings but by the usefulness of its words. THE SAME. Four fishermen are called, Simon, Andrew, James and John: leaving all things they follow. By this four-horse chariot we are carried to the heavens, etc., up to: we are covered with the skins of Solomon, in which the bride glories that she is beautiful. BEDA. It is asked how he called first Peter and Andrew and after a little James and John, as he narrates, etc., up to: for then, the ships not drawn up on land as with a care of returning, but as following one calling and commanding, they followed. And they enter. HIER. Mark, arranging the sayings of the Gospel in himself, not following the order of the history, keeps the order of the mysteries, hence on the sabbaths he narrates the first miracle, saying: And they enter, etc. Capharnaum. THE SAME. Capharnaum, village of consolation, the sabbath rest. The man in an unclean spirit, the human race, in which is uncleanness, etc., up to: Pharao dismissed by Israel, we pursue him, the despised devil rises into scandals. BEDA. That he especially heals and teaches on the sabbath shows that he is not under the law but above it: and he teaches us the true sabbath, that, namely, being intent on the salvation of souls, we abstain from every servile work, that is, from all unlawful things.
1.22: 1.22 For he was teaching them, etc. BEDA. The scribes said what was written in Moses and the prophets; Jesus, as God and Lord, freely added or changed what was lacking in the law of Moses himself; hence in Matthew: You have heard that it was said to them of old, etc. But I say to you.
1.24: 1.24 What have we to do with thee, etc. THE SAME. This is not a confession of will, but an extortion of necessity: as a runaway slave fears his master when he sees him, and begs off from blows. For the demons, seeing the Lord on earth, believed that they were at once to be judged.
1.25: 1.25 Hold thy peace. THE SAME. In fitting order the serpent tongue, which first scattered poison, is first shut that it may not scatter more, then, etc., up to: that the order of restoration in the Lord may be the same as that of perdition in the first-formed man.
1.26: 1.26 Tearing him. THE SAME. Or convulsing, as some codices have. But Luke says that it did him no harm. But what Mark says, tearing, is the same as Luke: when he had thrown him in the midst. And what he added, and did him no hurt: it is to be understood that that throwing down did not weaken him, as demons depart with some limbs cut off or torn away. THE SAME. By the man freed from the demon we understand the mind purified from unclean thought. By the woman cured of fevers, consequently, the flesh restrained from the fever of concupiscence by the precepts of continence.
1.27: 1.27 What thing is this? Through what they see they are aroused to inquire into what they had heard. For to this end the Lord himself works signs, and gave his disciples the power to work them, that through this the Gospel may be more surely believed, when those who promise heavenly things to earthly men work heavenly and divine works on earth.
1.30: 1.30 And forthwith they tell him, etc. Luke says that they asked for her. For the Savior heals now when asked, now of his own accord, to show that, even against the passions of vices, he is always present to the prayers of the faithful, and either gives understanding of what is not understood, or devoutly forgives what is not understood to those who ask. Hence: Who understandeth sins? from my secret ones cleanse me Psal. 18..
1.31: 1.31 Taking her. Peter's mother-in-law, sick with fever, is lifted up, taken by the hand. The fever is intemperance, from which we, sons of the Synagogue, are healed by the hand of discipline and the lifting up of desire, and we minister to the will of him who heals us as he declines toward evening from us. She ministered to them. BEDA. Tropologically: that is, let the members which served uncleanness serve justice.
1.32: 1.32 And when it was evening. THE SAME. The setting of the sun is the death of Christ. They brought to him all that were ill. For he healed more through the apostles after his death than when living in the flesh he preached to the Jews.
1.33: 1.33 At the door. HIER. The door of the kingdom is morally penance with faith, which works salvation for various infirmities. For various are the vices by which the city of the world languishes.
1.34: 1.34 Because they knew him. BEDA. Luke says more clearly: Devils went out from many, etc., because they knew that he was Christ. The demons therefore know that he is Christ and the Son of God, etc., up to: hence Paul: None of the princes of this world knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory I Cor. 2..
1.35: 1.35 And very early. THE SAME. As by the setting of the sun death, so by the dawn the resurrection of Christ, by whose manifest light he went into the desert of the Gentiles and prayed in the faithful, because he stirred their hearts to prayer.
1.38: 1.38 For to this purpose am I come. VICT. ANT. The evangelist adds this fittingly. For not only the authority of his divinity is overshadowed by this, but also the humility of his voluntary emptying. But Luke, to express the economy of the Word, writes, for therefore am I sent. Wherefore he designates the good pleasure of the Father about the incarnation of the Word by the name of apostleship.
1.39: 1.39 And he was preaching in their synagogues. BEDA. In this preaching is understood also that sermon given on the mount which Matthew relates; for, etc., up to: And behold a leper came and adored him, saying: Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst make me clean Matth. 8..
1.40: 1.40 And kneeling down, etc. BEDA. Humble and bashful. For everyone ought to blush for the stains of his life, but shame should not suppress confession: let him show the wound, ask the remedy. HIER. The leper, kneeling and entreating the Lord's will, is cleansed, who wills not the death of a sinner, but, etc., up to: Give alms: and behold all things are clean unto you. Luc. 11.. BEDA. The leper signifies the human race, which, according to Luke, is said to have been full of leprosy. For all, etc., up to: and truly to offer to the priest their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God Rom. 12.. If thou wilt, thou canst. THE SAME. In the will he ascribes the power, nor does he doubt as an unbeliever about the Lord's will, but, conscious of his foulness, he does not presume. THE SAME. He who, shut out from the Lord's law, asks to be cured by his power, judges that grace is above the law. For as in the Lord there is authority of power, so in him constancy of faith.
1.41: 1.41 Stretching forth his hand. THE SAME. The law forbids touching a leper, but because he is Lord of the law, he does not obey the law, but makes the law. He does not touch because he could not cure without touch, but proves thus that he was not subject to the law. I will, be thou made clean. THE SAME. This is wonderful, that he heals in the manner in which he is asked. I will, be thou made clean: and when he had said it, immediately the leprosy departed from him. Nothing between work and command. He spoke and they were made Psal. 32.. You see that will is power. Therefore, etc., up to: For he says, I will, on account of Photinus, he commands on account of Arius, he touches on account of Manichaeus.
1.44: 1.44 See, etc. THE SAME. Not that he wished what he could not, because he hath done all things whatsoever he would Psal. 113.. But he teaches that our benefits are to be restrained, not only from the reward of money, but also of favor. Shew thyself, etc. THE SAME. That he may understand that he was cured not by the order of the law, but by grace which is above the law. He commands him to offer, to show that he does not dissolve the law but fulfills it, while walking according to the law he heals above the law those whom the remedies of the law did not heal. Nor ought the sacrifice, being significant, to cease, when the thing signified was not yet confirmed by the constitution of the apostles and the faith of believers.
1.45: 1.45 But he being gone out. THE SAME. The salvation of one drives many to the Lord. He cannot be silent about the benefit, even when bidden by him who gave it. The Lord commanded it to be hidden. For he wishes that in the good things we do we wish to be hidden, which is of humility; and that we be betrayed against our will for the profit of others, which is of great loftiness, since even if we ourselves wish it, works cannot be kept silent. So that now, etc. HIER. Jesus was not manifested to all, who serve broad and plane-tree praises and their own pleasures, but to those, etc., up to: whom nothing can separate from the charity of God.
2.2: 2.2 So that there was no room, etc. BEDA. When the Lord preaches, they are not contained in the house, nor at the door: because when Christ preached in Judea the Gentiles did not yet wish to enter to hear, yet to them (though placed outside) he directed the words of his doctrine through his preachers.
2.3: 2.3 A man sick of the palsy. HIER. Palsy is a type of the torpor in which the sluggish man lies in the softness of the flesh, having a desire of salvation: but the crowds, etc., up to: that he may return to his own country by another way with the Magi. Carried by four. BEDA. Because by four virtues the confidence of the mind is raised to the Lord. Of which it is said in the book of Wisdom: She teacheth temperance and wisdom and justice and fortitude Sap. 8., which others call prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice.
2.4: 2.4 They uncovered the roof where he was. The roof of the house in which Christ teaches is the sublimity of Scripture, in which a young man corrects his way, in keeping thy words Psal. 118.. BEDA. The house of Jesus, according to another evangelist, is said to be covered with tiles, because the spiritual sense is covered by the lowliness of the letter. He is let down with his bed before Jesus, because he ought to know Jesus even while placed in this flesh.
2.5: 2.5 And when Jesus had seen. THE SAME. Much does one's own faith avail with God, where another's availed so much: that the man healed within and without suddenly rose, and by the merits of others his own sins were forgiven him. Son. Wonderful humility: him despised by all, loosened in all his limbs, he calls son. Or certainly for this reason, because his sins are forgiven him.
2.6: 2.6 Thy sins are forgiven thee. He shows that he was struck with the disease on account of sins, and therefore could not be healed unless these were first forgiven. As to the paralytic at the pool: Behold thou art made whole, sin no more, lest some worse thing happen to thee Joan. 5.. BEDA. For five causes men are afflicted with the troubles of the flesh. Either for increase of merits, as Job and the martyrs. Or for humility, etc., up to: Lazarus, whose sickness was not unto death, but for the glory of God, or for the beginning of eternal damnation, as Herod.
2.7: 2.7 Who can forgive sins. THE SAME. They say truly: God alone can do this, and he alone also forgives through those to whom he has given the power of forgiving sins, therefore he is truly God. They testify the truth, but are deceived by denying the person of Christ. They err therefore, because they believe that he is God and forgives sins, yet do not believe that he is Christ. But more madly the Arians, who dare not deny that he is Christ and forgives sins, yet do not fear to deny that he is God.
2.9: 2.9 Which is easier. THE SAME. As if to say: By the power by which I see hidden things of the heart, by the same I forgive sins. As if to say: Understand from yourselves what the paralytic obtains.
2.10: 2.10 The Son of man. THE SAME. God alone forgives sins, and the Son of man has power to forgive sins: therefore the same is God and the Son of man. Thus the man Christ forgives sins through the divinity, through the humanity can die for sinners.
2.11: 2.11 Go into thy house. THE SAME. He who was sick carries his bed home, when the soul, cured by the forgiveness of sins, brings itself back with the body itself to a lasting guard of itself: lest he again commit anything for which he may be struck.
2.13: 2.13 And he went forth, etc. THE SAME. After the cure of the paralytic in Capharnaum he goes out to the sea, because he instructs not only citizens but also the dwellers of the sea, and the wave-tossed motions of the world by firmness of faith, etc., up to: and draws them, separated from the waves of cupidities, to solitude, to the quiet of conversation which is in the hope of heavenly things.
2.14: 2.14 Levi. HIER. Levi, added, because from the tax office of secular business he follows the word alone which he says: for he that doth not renounce all that he possesseth, cannot be my disciple Luc. 14.. BEDA. Mark and Luke, for modesty and out of honor to the evangelist, do not put his commonly known name. He himself (according to what is written: The just man is first accuser of himself Prov. 18.) names himself Matthew and publican: to show that no convert ought to despair of salvation when an apostle and evangelist was suddenly made of a publican. He followed him. THE SAME. Luke more fully: And leaving all things, he followed him Luc. 5.. He follows, who, that he may be able to follow the poor Christ not so much with the step of the body as with the affection of the mind, leaves all things, etc., up to: deservedly therefore he who by obeying despised human business was made a dispenser of divine talents.
2.15: 2.15 And it came to pass. THE SAME. Luke: And Levi made him a great feast in his own house Luc. 5.. For he who receives Christ within delights in an abundance of pleasures, and the Lord gladly enters, and reclines in his affection. This is the spiritual feast of good poor men, in which the rich man is in want, the poor man feasts. Publicans. Those who exact public taxes, or who pursue worldly gains, who by the example of the converted publican now presume on salvation, not remaining in vices as the Pharisees calumniate, but penitent. BEDA. He goes to the feast of sinners: that he may have occasion of teaching, and impart spiritual food. By going to sinners the Lord's humility is shown: in the conversion of the penitent the power of his doctrine is evident. THE SAME. Through the calling of Matthew, the faith of the Gentiles: who, leaving the gains of the world, feast with the Lord at the banquets of charity and good works. Through the haughtiness of the Pharisees, the envy of the Jews at the salvation of the Gentiles is designated, to whom it is said: The publicans and harlots shall go into the kingdom of God before you Matth. 21..
2.17: 2.17 They that are well need not. THE SAME. If he speaks of a physician, he who by a wonderful kind of healing was wounded for our iniquities, and by his bruises we are healed Isa. 53..
2.18: 2.18 And the disciples. THE SAME. The other evangelists say that the Pharisees and the disciples of John asked this. Here he seems to say that others asked, whom concern for the same matter had moved. Hence it is gathered that this was objected by many, by the Pharisees, by the disciples of John, by the guests, or any others. THE SAME. The disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, because those who glory in the works of the law, or (what is worse) follow traditions, etc., up to: he ate with sinners, that seeing the grace you might acknowledge the power.
2.19: 2.19 Can the children. Matthew thus: Can the children of the bridegroom mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them, etc. Matth. 9. The bridegroom is Christ, the bride the Church, from which spiritual wedlock the apostles were begotten, who cannot mourn and fast as long as they see the bridegroom with the bride. When the wedding shall have passed, and the time of the passion and resurrection shall have come, then they shall fast. BEDA. As long as the bridegroom is with us, we are in joy, and can neither fast nor mourn; but when he withdraws and flies away on account of sin, then fasting is to be proclaimed, then mourning to be multiplied.
2.21: 2.21 No man seweth a piece. THE SAME. He calls the disciples old garments, that is, still carnal, not yet renewed by firmness of faith, etc., up to: wine, the fervor of faith, hope and charity, by which in the sight of God we are inwardly reformed by newness of mind.
2.22: 2.22 But new wine. They were new, however, when after the ascension they were renewed by hoping and praying for his consolation: then they received the Holy Spirit, with whom, as with new must, the new bottles were filled.
2.23: 2.23 On the sabbath. BEDA. Note first that the apostles uphold the letter of the sabbath against the Ebionites, who, while they receive other disciples, reject Paul as a transgressor of the law. And to pluck the ears. They hunger as men, having no time to eat because of the crowd. But they give an example of a more austere life, seeking not prepared feasts but simple food. BEDA. The disciples pass through the cornfields when prelates look around on their subjects with pious solicitude, and how to draw each to the faith, diligently, etc., up to: this the Lord of the sabbath approves, the foolish defenders of the sabbath disapprove, who love only the surface of the letter, know not the refreshment of the mind, know not the rest of souls.
2.25: 2.25 Have you never read, etc. Before others he brings forward David, who might seem to have opposed the sanctity of the law. He does this with the purpose that, through the honor and reverence which they paid to David, he may check the shameless sycophancy which they maliciously aimed at the apostles. As if he said: Do you not remember David bound by the servitude of the law? But I, though I am called Son of man, am Lord of the sabbath.
2.26: 2.26 Under Abiathar, etc. Be not troubled that others say Achimelech, for both were there at that time. Achimelech the father, and Abiathar the son: who, his father having been killed by Saul, became the companion of David's exile, and while he reigned was high priest of greater name than his father: and therefore worthy that the Lord should mention him, as the high priest, even while his father lived. The loaves of proposition. BEDA. As if to say: If David and Achimelech are not reproved by us, but are excused on account of hunger, why do you disapprove in these the cause which you approve in the others? although it be, etc., up to: and all the sons of the Church are priests, joined in a holy priesthood, offering themselves spiritual sacrifices to God. And gave to them. Following this: I will have mercy, and not sacrifice Ose. 6.: he judged it better to free men from the danger of hunger than to offer sacrifice. A victim pleasing to God is the salvation of men.
2.27: 2.27 The sabbath was made for man. BEDA. The sabbath is commanded to be kept in such a way that if there be necessity, one is not guilty, etc., up to: if a sick man breaks a fast, he is not held guilty.
2.28: 2.28 Therefore the Son of man. As if to say: If David the king and the priests (according to another evangelist), violating the sabbath on account of the temple's ministry, are free of crime, how much more the Son of man, true King and Priest! and therefore the Lord of the sabbath is not held guilty of the crime of the plucked ears on the sabbath.
3.1: 3.1 A withered hand. BEDA. The hand which was stretched out to the forbidden fruit withered from good work, restored by the hands of Christ stretched out on the cross to the juices of good works. HIER. This man signifies the covetous, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive, to plunder and not to bestow: to whom it is said to stretch out their hands, that is, let him that stole, steal no more, but rather let him labor, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have something to give to him that suffereth need Ephes. 4..
3.2: 3.2 And they watched him. BEDA. Because he had reasonably excused the disciples, they watch him, that if he cures on the sabbath they may accuse him of transgression, if he does not cure, of cruelty or weakness. Is it lawful on the sabbath to do good. THE SAME. He reproves that they violate the precepts of the law by a perverse interpretation, supposing that on the sabbath one must rest from good, when the law says, etc., up to: he put forward the similitude of the sheep, and concluded that it is lawful to do good on the sabbath. A life. THE SAME. He signifies the whole man by a part. Or because he did this for the sake of the soul, or because the healing of this hand signifies the salvation of the soul. To destroy. THE SAME. Not that the supremely pious can destroy anyone, but not to save him is to destroy. As it is said he hardened Pharao's heart, not that he hardened it, but that he did not soften it when hardened.
3.5: 3.5 Stretch forth thy hand. BEDA. The unfruitful weakness of the soul is not better cured than by the bestowal of alms; hence: He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none: and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner Luc. 3.. And in Ecclesiasticus: Let not thy hand be stretched out to receive, and shut when thou shouldst give Eccl. 4.. For in vain does he spread out his hands to the Lord in prayer who does not stretch them out to the widow asking. And his hand was restored to him. They reckon the great zeal of malice as a crime, that at his word the hand was healed. Nor can he be convicted of having worked on the sabbath who spoke and they were made: while they themselves on the sabbath carry food, hand out cups, and the other necessaries of living.
3.6: 3.6 And the Pharisees going out. Those who cannot by themselves seek partners in iniquity. With the Herodians. The ministers of Herod, because of the enmities which he himself exercised against the man, pursued with plots and hatred Jesus, whom John preached.
3.7: 3.7 Withdrew. He flees as a man, because his hour had not yet come, and there was no place for his passion outside Jerusalem. BEDA. He withdraws from the synagogue to the sea, etc. He leaves Judea, comes to the Gentiles with his disciples, that is, by the apostles preaching he approached the hearts of the Gentiles: and so he received many coming to him, and gave the desired salvation. And a great multitude. THE SAME. The masters of the people and the ministers of the king pursue with hatred: the unlearned crowd follows with love, and very many merit to be healed.
3.9: 3.9 A small ship. The Church gathered from the Gentiles, having passed the waves of the world in mind: which, the more it widens the bosom of the heart for receiving grace, the more securely it tramples the waves of the world. Lest they should press him. They press who disturb the peace of the Church. They touch who receive the faith with a true heart and love, who are said to have been healed when they touched: fleeing those who press, he goes up into the little ship.
3.11: 3.11 And the unclean spirits, etc. BEDA. Both those having plagues, and unclean spirits. But the infirm with pious intention of health: the possessed, or rather the demons in them: compelled by fear not only to fall down but also to confess his majesty. For, terrified by his presence, they could not hide him whom they knew already to be the Son of God. Saner than the Arians, who even today deny that he is the Son of God.
3.12: 3.12 That they should not make him known. THE SAME. Not only the demons, who unwillingly, or healed by him, who willingly confess: but even the apostles, who after the passion were to preach in the whole world, are commanded before the passion to be silent, lest, the divine majesty being preached, the passion be put off, and so the salvation of the world.
3.13: 3.13 And going up. THE SAME. After he forbade the unclean spirits to proclaim him, he chose holy men who would preach him and cast out the abominable spirits. This mountain signifies the height of justice, in which they were to be instructed, and which they were to preach, by the place he admonishes them to be raised to heavenly things, and so he gave the law on a mountain. HIER. It is the custom of divine Scripture to speak allegorically: but let us so apply high things to our senses that the truth of history, etc., up to: into the mountain the high are called, both by merit and by word, that the place may be congruous to high merits.
3.14: 3.14 That they might be twelve. God loved the beauty of Jacob when the Most High saw the nations and separated the sons of Adam. He set the bounds of peoples according to the number of the children of Israel, that they may sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. To them was given the power which the Son received from the Father according to the flesh, that the works which he did they also may do, and greater than these they may do. BEDA. He also gave power of raising the dead, as Matthew says, that the power shown may faith, etc., up to: because tongues are for a sign not to the faithful, but to unbelievers I Cor. 14..
3.16: 3.16 And he gave. THE SAME. Not only the first time, but when brought by Andrew he said: Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is interpreted Peter Joan. 1.. But here the evangelist makes you attentive, saying that, etc., up to: or hearing the sadness of death, namely when it is said to him: Another shall gird thee, and lead thee whither thou wouldst not I Cor. 4..
3.17: 3.17 And James. Who has supplanted the desires of the flesh. And John, who received by grace what others by labor. And he gave them the name Boanerges, which is the sons of thunder. Whose sublime merit deserves to hear on the mountain the thunder of the Father through the cloud concerning the Son: This is my beloved Son Matth. 17., that through the cloud of flesh they too might scatter the fire and lightnings of Christ in rain upon the earth. For the Lord made lightnings into rain, that mercy may extinguish what judgment burns; hence: Mercy and judgment I will sing to thee, O Lord Psal. 100.. James. Who, at the Lord's call, supplanted care of the flesh, and despised the flesh itself when Herod slaughtered. John. BEDA. In whom is grace, or the grace of the Lord, who for the grace of special love which he merited by virginal glory, leaned on the breast of his Redeemer in the passion. Sons. THE SAME. Of whom one, thundering, sent forth the theological voice (which no one before had known how to utter): In the beginning was the Word, etc. Joan. 1. This he left laden with such weight that if he had willed to thunder somewhat more, the world itself could not have contained it.
3.18: 3.18 And Andrew. HIER. Who manfully does violence to his own perdition, that he may always have in himself the answer of death and always have his soul in his hands. And Philip. THE SAME. Who is the mouth of a lamp, who illuminates by mouth what he received, to whom is given the work of an illuminated mouth. This kind of speech Scripture often records, when names are given on account of mysteries: which the evangelist now inserts, strongly affected by the person of God. And Bartholomew. THE SAME. Who is the son of him that suspends the waters, namely of him who said: I will command my clouds to rain no rain Isa. 5.. But the name of son of God is acquired through peace and love: For blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called the children of God Matth. 5.. And: Love your enemies that you may be the children of God Luc. 6.. And Matthew. Who is given: to whom is given not only remission of sins, but also to be in the number of apostles, that the lion and the ox may eat together, and the wolf with the lamb Isa. 11.. Note that the other evangelists put Matthew first, and do not call him publican. He puts himself after Thomas, and calls himself publican. And Thomas. THE SAME. Who is an abyss. For many know deep things but do not utter them. Hence I know a man in Christ, etc., up to: which it is not granted to man to utter II Cor. 12.. BEDA. Thomas, abyss: because he penetrated the depth of power in the resurrection. Or twin, which in Greek is called didymus, that is, doubtful because of a doubting heart, because he scarcely believed the resurrection. And James of Alpheus. That is, of the learned or the thousandth, from whose side a thousand shall fall, and ten thousand at thy right hand Psal. 90.. BEDA. James of Alpheus, who is also called brother of the Lord: because Mary was the sister of Alpheus, etc., up to: after the resurrection he was at once ordained bishop of Jerusalem, as learned or son of the learned. Thaddeus. Guardian of the heart. Luke in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles names him Jude of James, because he is brother of James the brother of the Lord. Hence he is called the son of Mary the mother of James and Joseph and Jude and Simon. HIER. And Thaddeus, who is little heart, that is, cultivator of the heart, who keeps his heart with all custody. For by cleanness of heart God is seen as through clean glass. And Simon. BEDA. Simon Cananean from Cana, a village of Galilee, who is also Simon Zelotes, that is, emulator. Cana, Zeal; Cananean, Zelotes. And Simon the Cananean. Who is also Zelotes, Simon, putting or having sadness. For blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted Matth. 5.. He fulfills a threefold mourning who seeks future consolation. He weeps for his own sins with David and Mary. With Paul he weeps with them that weep. And he weeps much with John who said: And I wept much: because no man was found worthy to open the book and to loose the seals thereof Apoc. 5.. But he is called Zelotes whom the zeal of the house of God hath eaten up, as Phinees: And the plague ceased Num. 25..
3.19: 3.19 And Judas Iscariot. He who does not blot out his sin by penance is not blotted out by memory either. Hence: And let the sin of his mother not be blotted out. Let them be before the Lord continually (Ps. 108). Judas means confessing or glorious; Scarioth means memory of death. Many confessors in the Church are proud and glorious, of whom the first is Simon Magus, and other heretics, whose deadly memory is celebrated in the Church, that it may be blotted out. JEROME. Judas Scarioth, named either from the village where he was born, or from the tribe of Issachar. Issachar means reward, namely the price of perdition. Scarioth, etc., up to those whom the example of one humbles to fear, as the fall of Lucifer does the angels, as in: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom (Jer. 9), but he that glories, let him glory in the Lord (1 Cor. 1). And they come, etc. BEDE. Those who have taken on the care of others must watch carefully over the gift of conscience, so that they may first govern themselves and then others.
3.20: 3.20 JEROME. The house in which they gather is the primitive Church. The crowds that prevent them from eating bread are sins and vices, because he who eats the body of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord (1 Cor. 11). Hence the Lord is turned to fury when he says: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life (John 6).
3.21: 3.21 And when they had heard, etc. The crowd throngs him, while his own despise him as if he were mad; in this the salvation of the Gentiles is indicated and the envy of the Jews is condemned, of whom it is said: He came unto his own, and his own received him not (John 6).
3.22: 3.22 And the Scribes. BEDE. If some, through slowness of mind, do not understand the word of God, there still remains hope of salvation; if perhaps they do understand, there is none. But those who refuse to understand and twist what they understand have no hope. Hence, the Scribes, that is, the wise, etc. From Jerusalem. This signifies that he would be pursued to death by his own citizens. We read above that a crowd followed him from Galilee and Jerusalem, and beyond the Jordan and about Tyre and Sidon, which are cities of the Gentiles; and the Scribes from Jerusalem blasphemed. For the crowd of the Jewish people led him with palms and praises; the Gentiles desired him; the Scribes and elders of the people plotted his death. He has Beelzebub. Lord of flies, or one having flies; by this name they called the prince of demons because of the filth of sacrificial blood.
3.23: 3.23 How can Satan, etc. BEDE. Let them choose what they wish. If Satan cannot cast out Satan, they say nothing against the Lord. But if he can, let them leave his kingdom, which, being divided, cannot stand.
3.27: 3.27 And then he will plunder his house. THE SAME. He plundered the house, because he distributed all the parts of the world possessed by the devil to the apostles and their successors, as if to divided provinces, that they might convert the peoples to the faith.
3.29: 3.29 But he that shall blaspheme. JEROME. Because he does not deserve to do penance so as to be received, who, understanding Christ, said that he was the prince of demons, etc., up to: For he that shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 5). BEDE. Matthew says (Matt. 12): He that shall blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, either word, etc. Here he shows that some sins are forgiven in the world to come. This is to be understood of the smallest sins, such as idle talk and excessive laughter, for which even this life has earned forgiveness. Never. This is against Origen, who promises pardon to all sinners after the judgment, once countless ages have passed. He shall be guilty of an everlasting sin. BEDE. Not because he says that the Spirit does not exist; or that he exists but is not God; or that he is God but less than the Father and the Son; since this comes not from diabolical envy but from human ignorance, etc.
3.31: 3.31 His brethren. JEROME. Not sons of Mary, ever Virgin, as Helvidius falsely claims; nor of Joseph by another wife, as others babble, but kinsmen. BEDE. The mother and brethren, the people of the Jews from whom Christ came according to the flesh, stand outside in the literal sense. The crowd in the house are the Gentiles in the spiritual mystery. The Jews want to see Christ outside, because, not seeking the spiritual understanding, they rather force him, or seek, to go out to teach carnal things.
3.33: 3.33 Who is my mother. THE SAME. He who says: Honor your father and your mother (Ex. 20) does not refuse to obey his mother, but shows that he owes more to the Father's mysteries than to maternal affections; he showed the same by example, which he said in word: He that loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10). Nor does he insultingly despise his brethren, but places spiritual work above kinship, teaching that the bond of hearts is better than that of bodies.
3.34: 3.34 Behold my mother, etc. JEROME. That we may know that we are both his brethren and his mother if we do the will of his Father, so that we may be coheirs, since he distinguishes not by sex but by deeds. One is a sister and brother by believing, a mother by preaching, when through preaching the love of Christ is, as it were, begotten like Christ himself in the heart of the hearer.
4.1: 4.1 And again he began to teach. BEDE. Going out from the house where he is said to have a demon, he teaches by the sea, to show that because of the guilt of unbelief he would leave Judea and pass over to the Gentiles. Hence it is fittingly stated beforehand that, while he preached in the house, his mother and brethren stood outside. JEROME. He began to teach by the sea, so that the place may indicate bitter and unstable hearers. And therefore, etc., up to him who sweetens what is bitter, turns sorrow into joy, sickness into health. Going up into a ship, etc. BEDE. The Church, which is in the sea among unbelievers, which God illumines by the grace of his visitation and consecrates as a dwelling beloved to himself. And all the multitude by the sea. JEROME. These are those who have recently come to hear the word, and from there, by devotion of soul, have followed from the bitterness of the reprobate as from the sea; but they are not yet with the Lord in the ship, because they have not yet been imbued with the heavenly mysteries or sacraments that they desire.
4.2: 4.2 In parables many things. A parable is a comparison, made under some likeness, of things differing in nature. He speaks according to his wisdom, so that those who could not grasp heavenly things might perceive them through an earthly likeness they heard. In Greek it is called a likeness when we indicate what we want understood by certain comparisons, as when we compare iron, a hard man, a swift man, to winds and birds. The same holds for the thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold fruit, that is, the law, the prophets and the Gospel, since the mystery of the kingdom, shown on the mountain, rests on the mouth of three witnesses, that is, Moses, Elijah and Jesus.
4.4: 4.4 Some fell by the way side, etc. Luke: And it was trodden down, and the birds of the air devoured it (Luke 8). The way is the mind, worn down by fear of carnal thoughts; hence the seed perishes and bears no fruit, and is snatched away by the birds, that is, by demons, who are called birds of the air, either because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they dwell in the air.
4.15: 4.15 And these, etc. He sets out the differences among those who hear the word. There are some, like the Gentiles, who do not hear at all.
4.19: 4.19 And the lusts after other things, etc. Which is commanded. For it is commanded: Desire wisdom: keep the commandments (Prov. 7), etc. And elsewhere: Blessed is the man that fears the Lord; he shall delight exceedingly in his commandments (Ps. 3). These are good desires; he who desires other things goes astray.
4.21: 4.21 A candle, etc. JEROME. The candle is the word of God. The bushel or bed is the hearing of the disobedient. The candlestick is the apostles, whom the word of God enlightened. The hidden and secret is what is made manifest when it is handled by the Lord. BEDE. The bushel is our life measured by divine foreknowledge. The bed is the flesh, in which, etc., up to because he puts the lusts of the flesh before it. Is it not to be set on a candlestick? THE SAME. So that the preaching of the truth may rule and the service of the body be subject, through which, however, the teaching appears the more exalted, as a candle does by a candlestick.
4.22: 4.22 For there is nothing, etc. As if he said: Do not be ashamed of the Gospel, because there is nothing hidden now that will not be made manifest at the judgment, when God will enlighten the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of hearts (Matt. 10); where there will be praise from God for you, but eternal punishment for them.
4.24: 4.24 With what measure, etc. JEROME. For according to the measure of faith the understanding of the mysteries is dealt out to each, and the gift of knowledge will be added to us, and virtues will also be added.
4.25: 4.25 For he that has, etc. That is, he who has faith will have power, and he who has the work of the word will have understanding of the mystery. And conversely, he who has not faith fails in power; and he who has not the work of the word lacks understanding of it; and he who does not understand loses his hearing, as if he had not heard.
4.26: 4.26 So is the kingdom of God. JEROME. Divine Scripture shows heavenly mysteries through earthly likenesses, as is plain throughout the whole body of the Gospels. The kingdom of God is the Church, which, etc., up to: Because the harvest is come, that is, the consummation of the world, in which the just who sowed in tears will rejoice.
4.29: 4.29 He puts in the sickle. VICTOR OF ANTIOCH. The harvest is the time of the consummation; the sickle of God is the word, more piercing than any two-edged sword. But the sickle in this place does not denote, etc., up to for all bear grain, though not all equally much.
4.31: 4.31 Like a grain. JEROME. He again compares this seed to a grain of mustard seed, which is the least in fear, great in charity, which is greater than all herbs, because God is charity, and all flesh is grass, and he who is weak, let him eat herbs. And it makes branches of mercy and compassion, under whose shade the poor of Christ, who are the creatures of heaven, delight to dwell. When it is sown. By Christ or by man, in the earth, or in the field, that is, in his own heart. This man is our understanding and mind, which, cherishing the grain of preaching, makes it sprout in the field of its heart with the moisture of faith. It is less, etc. Since he preaches things that seem contemptible, he is at first not believed, because he preaches God a man who died, crucified; compared with the eloquence and wisdom of the philosophers, this is found to be less.
4.32: 4.32 It goes up, etc. It surpasses the nature of herbs in height, breadth and age: it is high, because it lifts up to heavenly things; broad, because it has filled the whole world; aged, because it cannot come to an end. Herbs. BEDE. The philosophical disciplines, which become the more worthless the more openly they grow, because like garden herbs they quickly wither.
4.34: 4.34 Without a parable. THE SAME. Not that he made no discourse plain to the crowds, but that no discourse of his is found in which there is not something of a parable. But apart, the disciples. JEROME. For those were worthy to hear the mysteries in the innermost shrine of wisdom who, with the tumult of thoughts set aside, remained in the solitude of the virtues. For wisdom is to be learned in time of leisure.
4.36: 4.36 In the ship. BEDE. Allegorically: the sea is the surge of the world. The little ship is the cross, by which we climb over the waves of the world and reach the shore of the heavenly homeland. Other ships, etc., up to for those ships were perhaps newly built and only brought into harbor, or brought back to harbor after the perils of the sea.
4.38: 4.38 In the stern. JEROME. The stern holds the living together with dead skins and keeps back the waves, and is made solid with wood, etc., up to: A great calm; the peace of the Church after tribulations, or the contemplative life after the active. Asleep. BEDE. Christ falls asleep while the disciples sail, because for the faithful who meditate on the rest of the kingdom to come, and who, with the second breath of the Holy Spirit or the oar of their own effort, cast the waves of the world behind them, the passion of Christ suddenly comes; at his ascending, etc., up to but let us run back to the helmsman, let us eagerly awaken him, who does not serve but commands the winds, who will calm all things, who will grant the harbor of salvation.
4.39: 4.39 Peace, be still. Note that every creature feels the command of the Creator. Not that all things are animate, as the heretics falsely claim, but by the majesty of the Maker, things that are insensible to us are sensible to him.
4.40: 4.40 Why are you fearful? BEDE. As if he said: Why do you fear while I am present? Like this is what he reproached after the resurrection, their unbelief and hardness of heart, because those who had seen him rise did not believe (Mark 16). And again: O foolish and slow of heart to believe in all things which the prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and so to enter into his glory? (Luke 24). And they feared. Matthew: But the men wondered, saying: What manner of man is this, etc. (Matt. 8). So it was not the disciples but others who were in the ship who wondered, doubting about him whom the sea and the wind obeyed. Or even the disciples themselves are rightly called men, because they did not yet know the power of the Savior.
5.1: 5.1 And they came, etc. BEDE. Gerasa, a notable city of Arabia, beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh, not far from the lake of Tiberias, in which the swine were drowned, signifies, etc., up to and he who was far off was made near in the blood of Christ.
5.2: 5.2 A man with an unclean spirit. ISIDORE. This most desperate man is the people of the Gentiles, whom the Apostle enumerates: haughty, proud, unclean, bloodthirsty, idolatrous, shameless, etc., up to for when the fool is scourged, the wise man becomes wiser or more prudent.
5.3: 5.3 And no man could bind him, not even with chains, etc. BEDE. By the heavy chains and fetters are signified the two laws of the Gentiles, by which sins in their public life were restrained. When the chains were broken (as Luke writes), he was suddenly driven by the devil into the desert, because even when those laws were transgressed they were carried off by desire to crimes which already exceeded common custom.
5.7: 5.7 That you torment me not. THE SAME. It is a great torment to him to cease from harming man, and he lets go the more painfully the longer he has possessed.
5.9: 5.9 What is your name? BEDE. He asks not as one who does not know, but so that, the plague he had endured being publicly confessed, the power of the healer may appear the more welcome. But even the priests of our time who cast out demons by exorcism are accustomed to say that sufferers cannot be cured otherwise unless, as far as they can recall, they openly confess everything they endured from demons, waking or sleeping, by sight, hearing, or any sense of body or mind. My name is Legion. THE SAME. It signifies the Gentile people enslaved to the countless cults of idolatry; to which, on the contrary, is, etc., up to but the wicked are confounded and divided by more sects than tongues.
5.12: 5.12 Send us. THE SAME. Luke: And they besought him that he would not command them to go out into the abyss (Luke 8). So they knew that at some time, by his coming, they would be sent into the abyss, not the things to come, etc., up to for unless someone has lived after the manner of a swine, the devil receives no power over him, except perhaps to test, not to destroy.
5.13: 5.13 The herd was cast down. BEDE. Because now that the Church is made glorious and the people of the Gentiles freed from the dominion of demons, they carry out sacrilegious rites in hidden places, etc., up to since for the salvation of one man two thousand swine are drowned.
5.14: 5.14 And they that fed them. Because certain leaders of the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim its power among the nations, in astonishment and wonder.
5.15: 5.15 And they see him. BEDE. Luke: Sitting at his feet. This signifies those who have been corrected from their sins, that with fixed attention of mind they gaze upon the footsteps of the Savior, which they are to follow. Clothed. With the pursuit of virtues, which he had lost in his frenzied mind. Hence the prodigal son returning to his father is soon clothed with the first robe and the ring, because whoever repents with a true heart can, by the granting grace of Christ, recover with the ring of unviolated faith the former works of justice from which he had fallen. And they were afraid. For many, delighted with their old pleasure, say they honor the Christian law but are unwilling to suffer for it, because they cannot fulfill it, yet they admire the faithful people healed from their former way of life.
5.17: 5.17 And they began to pray him. RABANUS. Like Peter: Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man, etc. (Luke 5). Or lest they touch the ark of God, like Uzzah.
5.19: 5.19 Go into your house. BEDE. So let each one, after the resurrection from sins, return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others, that afterward he may rest with Christ, lest in wishing to be with Christ too hastily he neglect the mystery of preaching, which is suited to the redemption of his brethren. JEROME. The healed man is sent into his house, that is, into the spiritual observance of the law; and he proclaims, etc., up to because moral precepts are to be observed according to the letter. BEDE. Matthew says two were cured of the demon, Mark and Luke one, because one of them was of more distinguished name, was more famous, and therefore his cure is more famous. Allegorically: the two signify the Gentiles, from the two sons of Noah. For though Noah begot three sons, one was taken into the possession of God, and two were given over to idols.
5.22: 5.22 And there comes one, etc. JEROME. After this Jairus, the ruler of the synagogue, comes, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel, etc., up to Abraham and Moses and Samuel pray for the dead people, and Jesus follows their prayers. BEDE. Jairus means enlightening or enlightened, because he enlightened the people with the words of life; and in order to be able to do this, he was enlightened by the Holy Spirit.
5.23: 5.23 My daughter. BEDE. Luke: For she was an only daughter, about twelve years old, and she was dying (Luke 8). The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the Synagogue, alone by legal instruction, etc., up to struck down suddenly by the languor of errors, she hopelessly abandoned the spiritual ways.
5.24: 5.24 And they thronged him. While he goes to heal the girl, he is pressed by the crowd, because, offering the Jews admonitions of salvation by which he might raise up their sick conscience, he was burdened by the harmful custom of the carnal peoples.
5.25: 5.25 And a woman, etc. While the Lord is going to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, a sick woman of twelve years snatches health beforehand, and afterward the daughter is healed and raised, because the salvation of the human race was so dispensed that first some of Israel, then the fullness of the Gentiles, and so all Israel will be saved. BEDE. It should be noted that the girl was twelve years old and the woman suffered from the flow of blood for twelve years, etc., up to while Christ was resolving to heal Judea, he forestalled, with sure hope, the salvation already prepared and promised to others.
5.26: 5.26 And had suffered many things, etc. THE SAME. From false theologians, philosophers, and teachers of secular laws, who promised to give useful precepts for living. The demons also, etc., up to they began both to hope for and to seek a remedy for their sickness.
5.27: 5.27 Came in the crowd. THE SAME. If any man serve me, let him follow me (John 12). And elsewhere: You shall walk after the Lord your God (Hosea 11). Or because she does not see God present in the flesh, but afterward comes to the grace of the recognition of faith, etc., up to by the Gospel sacraments, as by his garments, he cleanses the foul fountains of blood.
5.31: 5.31 Touched. BEDE. Only the faithful woman touches the Lord, whom the crowd, accompanying him on all sides, presses. Because he who is weighed down by the heresies of those who crowd together in disorder, or by perverse morals, is touched only by the faithful heart of the Church; hence: Do not touch me, for I am not yet ascended to my Father (John 20). Because to touch him truly is to believe him equal to the Father. JEROME. The dead girl is raised by the seventh power, but along the way the woman with the flow of blood touches the hem from behind, who together with her health, etc., up to the cymbal, confession; the pomegranate signifies the willingness for martyrdom and the whiteness of the virtues.
5.33: 5.33 But the woman. BEDE. See to what the question was tending, that the woman might confess the truth of her long illness and of her sudden belief and healing, and so be herself strengthened in faith and give an example to others.
5.35: 5.35 Yet speaking, etc. BEDE. As soon as the woman is healed, it is announced that the girl is dead, because the Church of the Gentiles, cured of the stain of vices and, by the merit of faith, etc., up to but what is impossible for men is possible for God.
5.36: 5.36 To the ruler of the synagogue. The ruler of the synagogue is the assembly of the teachers of the law, of whom it is said: The scribes and the Pharisees have sat in the chair of Moses (Matt. 28). If they are willing to believe, the Synagogue subject to them will also be saved.
5.37: 5.37 And he admitted not, etc. BEDE. The mysteries are not to be revealed to blasphemers and mockers, but to the faithful who honor them. Hence elsewhere: Wisdom is justified by all her children (Matt. 11).
5.38: 5.38 Weeping and wailing. THE SAME. Let all that hope in you be glad; they shall rejoice for ever, and you shall dwell in them (Ps. 5). The Synagogue has lost this joy by the merit of unbelief, and therefore lies dead among those weeping and wailing. But Jesus does not allow her to perish utterly.
5.39: 5.39 She is not dead. To me, in whose disposition her soul lives, received, and her flesh, to be raised, rests. Hence it is the custom of Christians that the dead who are not doubted to be going to rise are called sleepers; hence: We would not have you ignorant, brethren, concerning them that are asleep (1 Thess. 4). BEDE. Although the soul that sins shall die, nevertheless one whom the Lord foresees for eternal life may, not inappropriately, be said to have been dead to us but to have fallen asleep to him.
5.40: 5.40 Having put them all out. THE SAME. The crowd is put out so that the girl may be raised, because unless the multitude of worldly cares is cast out of the heart, the soul that lies dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself among all manner of thoughts, it in no way gathers itself to consider itself.
5.41: 5.41 Talitha cumi. In the Syriac speech which the evangelist gives, it is no more than: Girl, arise. But perhaps to express the force of the Lord's command he added this: I say to you, arise, and took care to convey the sense of the speaker rather than the words. So the apostles and evangelists often, when they take up some testimony, give the sense rather than the words. JEROME. To the girl it is said Talitha cumi, that is, Girl, arise. To the ruler of the synagogue, etc., up to hence it is said: Abraham believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice (James 2). BEDE. That Christ raised three dead persons signifies three kinds of souls. He raises the girl, etc., up to the fourth dead man heard it announced by the disciple; but because there were no living to pray for him, he said: Let the dead bury their dead (Matt. 8).
6.2: 6.2 From where has this man, etc. Wonderful blindness. In his deeds and words they can recognize Christ; they despise him only because they know his family.
6.3: 6.3 The carpenter. BEDE. He who works with fire and spirit; hence: He shall baptize you with fire and the Spirit (John 1). He is the craftsman who fashioned the dawn and the sun.
6.4: 6.4 A prophet is not without honor. It is almost natural for fellow citizens to envy fellow citizens, because they remember not the works but the childhood they have seen. ISIDORE. Lowliness often accompanies origin. As: Who is the son of Jesse? (3 Kings 12). But: The Lord looks on the humble, and the high he knows afar off (Ps. 137).
6.5: 6.5 And he could not, etc. Lest by working many miracles he should condemn the unbelieving citizens the more. Or because he is despised in his own country, he worked few miracles and signs there, so that they might not be wholly without excuse. He works greater signs daily among the Gentiles, not so much in the healing of bodies as of souls.
6.6: 6.6 And he wondered. BEDE. Not as if surprised, but he shows it as a thing to be wondered at, that they believe neither the prophets nor him whom they see present.
6.7: 6.7 And he called. JEROME. The twelve apostles are sent, and power is given them to teach the precepts, so that word and deed may go together, and that powers may be joined with invisible promises, and so, when they anoint the sick with oil, they strengthen the weakness of faith by power. And he gave them, etc. The kind Lord and master does not begrudge his disciples and servants his power. But he himself acts by his own power; they act by their weakness, if they do anything, and confess the power of the Lord, saying: In the name of Jesus arise and walk (Acts 3).
6.8: 6.8 That they should take nothing, etc. Let there be such trust in the Lord that they know most certainly that nothing is lacking, lest, while they provide for themselves temporal things, they provide less for others the eternal. BEDE. Matthew and Luke record that the Lord told his disciples to carry not even a staff; Mark, that they should take nothing but a staff. But they actually receive a staff. Mark understands by the staff the power of receiving necessities from those they serve.
6.9: 6.9 But to be shod with sandals. THE SAME. So that the foot may be neither covered nor bare to the ground, that is, that the Gospel be neither hidden nor rest on earthly comforts. Nor put on two coats. THE SAME. This means that they should walk simply, not doubly.
6.11: 6.11 Shake off the dust from your feet. THE SAME. The dust is shaken off the feet as a testimony of their labor, that they entered the city, that the preaching reached them. Or that they received nothing from those who despised the Gospel for necessary sustenance.
6.13: 6.13 And anointed with oil. THE SAME. James says: Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil (James 5), etc. Hence it is clear that this custom was handed down from the apostles, that the possessed and other sick persons be anointed with oil consecrated by a bishop.
6.14: 6.14 And king Herod heard. THE SAME. Luke (Luke 9): Now Herod the tetrarch heard of all things that were done by him, etc. Hence it must be understood that either, strengthened by the words of others, he said it in belief, or still hesitating, etc., up to had not risen again, but preferred to believe he had been secretly carried away.
6.17: 6.17 Of Philip his brother. BEDE. The old history relates that Philip was a son of Herod the elder, and brother of the Herod under whom the Lord suffered, and that he had married Herodias, the daughter of Aretas; and that afterward, when enmities arose, Aretas took back his daughter and joined her in marriage to Herod, Philip's enemy, to Philip's grief. Hegesippus or Josephus, however, tell it quite differently.
6.18: 6.18 It is not lawful for you, etc. THE SAME. He who had come in the spirit and power of Elijah rebuked Herod and Herodias, as, etc., up to for man is born to labor, and the saints pass through death to rest.
6.23: 6.23 And he swore. BEDE. He is not excused from perjury by the oath. For perhaps he swore precisely in order to find an occasion for killing. And if she had asked for the death of her father or mother, Herod would certainly not have granted it.
6.26: 6.26 And the king was struck sad, etc. THE SAME. Sad in the customary manner of Scripture, not in fact but in the opinion of many. As also Joseph himself, etc., up to so that under the pretext of piety he became impious.
6.27: 6.27 His head in a dish. THE SAME. The head of the law, which is Christ, is cut off from the body, etc., up to but Christ, who is the light of the world, when the days begin to grow longer.
6.29: 6.29 And took. THE SAME. Josephus relates that John was bound, led to the fortress of Machaerus, and beheaded there. Ecclesiastical history relates that it was in the city of Sebaste in Palestine, once called Samaria. But in the time of Julian, etc., up to when the temple of Serapis had been cleansed of its filth, he placed the same bones there and consecrated a basilica in honor of Saint John.
6.30: 6.30 And the apostles coming together. JEROME. They return to the place from which the rivers go forth. They always give thanks to God for what they have received. All things. Not only what the apostles themselves had done and taught do they report to the Lord, but also what John suffered while they were teaching. Or the disciples of themselves or of the same John, as Matthew writes.
6.31: 6.31 Come apart. BEDE. Not only for the sake of seeking rest, but mystically it signifies that, having left Judea, which, etc., up to he comes apart, leads those whom he chooses, so that among those who live badly they may not attend to evil things, as Lot in Sodom, and Job in the land of Hus, and Obadiah in the house of Ahab. Rest. As the birds in the branches of the mustard. Small is the rest here for the saints, long the labor; but afterward it is said to them that they may rest from their labors. For there were, etc. JEROME. In Noah's ark the animals that were inside were sent out, and those that were outside burst in. So in the Church Judas, etc., up to then the wind and storm will cease, with Jesus sitting and reigning in the ship, which is the universal Church.
6.32: 6.32 They went into a desert place. BEDE. By seeking solitude he tests whether the faith of the crowds will follow him, and rewards it, once tested, with fitting recompense. The crowds take the way of the desert not on beasts of burden or in carriages, but by the labor of their own feet, and show their desire for salvation. Again he himself, by receiving the weary, teaching the ignorant, healing the sick, refreshing the fasting, indicates how much he is delighted by the devotion of those who believe.
6.33: 6.33 And on foot. Note that they did not reach the other bank of the sea without a boat across the Jordan. But having crossed some strait or lake, they came to the nearest places of the same region, to which even natives on foot could come.
6.34: 6.34 And he had compassion. BEDE. How he had compassion Matthew explains more fully thus: And he had compassion on them, and healed their sick. For this is truly to have compassion on the poor and those having no shepherd: to open the way of truth, to heal the sick, and by feeding the fasting to encourage them to praise the heavenly bounty; the things that follow show that he did these.
6.35: 6.35 And when the hour was now far spent. As the day declined the Savior refreshed the crowds, because either with the end of the world drawing near, or when the sun of justice set for us, we were freed from the long hunger of spiritual want. BEDE. Many companies of the faithful, leaving behind the walls of their former way of life and neglecting the defense of various doctrines, follow Christ as he seeks the deserts of the Gentiles; and although God was first known in Judea, then his glory was exalted above the heavens and above all the earth.
6.37: 6.37 Give them. He challenges the apostles to the breaking of bread so that, when they testify that they have not got it, the greatness of the sign might be made known. And he hints that hearts that fast are to be fed daily through them, when by their examples or words we are roused to love heavenly things. It should be noted that John, when about to write of this miracle of the loaves, put first that the Pasch was near. Matthew and Mark say this happened immediately after John was killed; from which it is gathered that John was beheaded when the Pasch was near, and that the Lord was crucified at the following Pasch.
6.38: 6.38 Five. BEDE. The five loaves are the five books of the Mosaic law, in which the knowledge of the divine eternity, the creation of the world, the course of the present age, and the true religion of serving God, etc., up to and at the last he gives to the elect, as a great gift, to eat and drink at his table in his kingdom.
6.39: 6.39 By companies. THE SAME. The different seatings are the distinct orders of the churches, which make one catholic Church.
6.40: 6.40 By hundreds and by fifties. By fifty, the rest of the jubilee. Fifty doubled makes a hundred, and so it signifies the perfection of both rests, namely of body and mind. For he who rests from evil acts has rest of body; but he who rests also from perverse thoughts has rest of mind. Well do those sitting on the green grass feed on the food of God who, by the pursuit of abstinence, having trampled the allurements of the flesh, give their effort to hearing and fulfilling the words of God. Therefore some are by fifties, others by hundreds, because one first rests from evil work, so that afterward there may be rest in the mind as well.
6.41: 6.41 And taking. He does not create new food, because, having become incarnate, he preaches nothing other than what was written, but shows that the law and the prophets are pregnant with mysteries. He broke. And he distributed to his disciples the food to be set before the crowds, because he opened the sacraments to the holy teachers, who were to preach them throughout the whole world.
6.43: 6.43 And they took up, etc. BEDE. The more secret mysteries which the unlearned cannot grasp, the more perfect diligently search out. For by the baskets are figured the twelve apostles, and the teachers who follow through the apostles, despised outside, within heaped with the remnants of saving food for nourishing the hearts of the humble. For in baskets servile tasks are carried out; but that bread of fragments filled them, which chose the weak things of the world to break or confound.
6.44: 6.44 Five thousand. THE SAME. On account of the five senses of the body. These, having followed the Lord, signify those who, still placed in secular life, know how to use well the external things they possess. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because it is necessary that such persons still be instructed by legal precepts. But those who renounce the world entirely are the four thousand refreshed with seven loaves, that is, lofty in evangelical perfection and taught inwardly by spiritual grace.
6.45: 6.45 And immediately he obliged. He gives us an example, that in all the good we do we should avoid the reward of human favor, lest the working of virtues bend us toward desire for temporal things. The Lord himself hints this to us, when those who marvelled at his miracles wanted to make him king, and he fled to the mountain to pray. He readily met his crucifiers, so that we may be ready to bear adversity, wary of flatteries if they smile, and implore the Lord with frequent prayers that they not deceive us by softening us, if they abound. To Bethsaida. BEDE. Bethsaida is a city in Galilee, of Andrew and Peter and Philip, near the lake of Genesareth. But Mark says, etc., up to both of which are cities in Galilee by the lake of Genesareth, which is also called of Tiberias, from the city of Tiberias.
6.46: 6.46 He went into the mountain. THE SAME. He prays well who seeks God in prayer, advancing from earthly things to higher, and ascends to the summit of the loftier court. He who from riches, etc., up to he can do all things he wills, because he is our advocate and judge; the one a duty of piety, the other a mark of power.
6.47: 6.47 And he alone, etc. He who sometimes seems altogether to have abandoned the Church in dangers; hence: Why, O Lord, have you retired afar off? (Ps. 10), etc. But though he delays help, he does not take away support.
6.48: 6.48 And about the fourth. BEDE. Military stations and watches are divided by spaces of hours; it is therefore clear that they, etc., up to for Lucifer is said to light three hours of the night, that is, the whole morning watch. And he would have passed by them. THE SAME. So that for an hour they were troubled, but, delivered at once, they might be the more amazed at the miracle of their deliverance, and their rescuer, etc., up to When you shall walk in the fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not burn in you;
6.49: 6.49 They thought. BEDE. Even now heretics think it was a phantom, and that he did not take true flesh from the virgin. For Theodorus, etc., up to and how he walked, without his feet being wet, on a moist and unstable substance, though having bodily weight and material burden.
6.50: 6.50 Fear not. The first help is to drive away fear; the second, to calm the storm by the power of his presence. Nor is it wonder if, when the Lord goes up into the ship, the wind ceases: for in whatever heart he is present by the grace of his love, soon all the wars of vices and of the opposing world and of malignant spirits are quieted.
6.52: 6.52 For they understood not. BEDE. By the miracle of the loaves he showed that he was the maker of things. By walking upon the waves, that he had his whole body free from every weight of sin. By calming the winds and waves, he showed that he ruled the elements. But the disciples, still carnal, were indeed amazed at the greatness of the powers, but did not recognize the truth of the divine majesty.
6.54: 6.54 They knew him. By report, not by face or by the greatness of the signs; he was known to very many even by his countenance.
6.56: 6.56 The hem of his garment. BEDE. The least commandment, which whoever shall break shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven; or the assumption of flesh, through which we come to the Word of God.
7.1: 7.1 And there assemble. THE SAME. It is clear how true is the Lord's confession to the Father, in which he says: Because you have hid these things from the wise and prudent, and have revealed them to little ones (Matt. 11). The unlearned come, bring the sick, that they may touch even the hem of his garment, and so receive the health they desired.
