But the Pharisees and Scribes, who ought to have been the teachers of the people, run together not to hear the word, not as to a physician, but to battles of questions.
7.2: 7.2 With common hands. JEROME. Unclean, or common hands signify communion with the Gentiles. The cleanness of the Pharisees is barren; the communion of the apostles does not wholly extend its branches to the sea. Not washed. They find fault about unwashed hands of the body, when nothing of uncleanness is found in their works. They, washed outwardly with water, are polluted within by the stain of conscience.
7.3: 7.3 The Pharisees. BEDE. It is a superstitious tradition of men to wash frequently before eating and the like. But the necessary teaching of truth bids those who desire to eat the bread of life which came down from heaven to purge their works frequently by the washing of almsgiving and other fruits of justice.
7.4: 7.4 Washings. In vain do they keep the washings of vessels who neglect the filth of their hearts and bodies. For this was not said of material hands, but for the cleansing of minds, and the correction of works, and the holiness and salvation of souls.
7.5: 7.5 Why do your disciples, etc. Wonderful folly! They accuse the Son of God because he does not keep the precepts of men. But the hands, that is, the works, of the soul, not of the body, are to be washed, that the Word of God may come to be in them.
7.6: 7.6 Well did he prophesy. JEROME. The barking of the Pharisees is held back by the fork of reason, that is, by the rebuke of Moses and Isaiah, so that we too can overcome heretics with the words of Scripture.
7.9: 7.9 Well do you make void. He refutes a false calumny with true reason, as if to say: You, for the sake of the tradition of men, despise and neglect the precepts of God; why then do you accuse my disciples, who make light of the commands of the elders in order to keep the commandments of God?
7.11: 7.11 But you say. BEDE. The Lord, taking account of the weakness of parents, whether of age or of poverty, commanded, etc., up to that the offering of the Lord, who is the true Father, be put first. It shall profit you. ISIDORE. What is consumed for your own uses, which is sacrilege. Or as a question. As if he said: Will it profit you? It ought not: fearing this, the fathers were afflicted with hunger.
7.15: 7.15 There is nothing from without, etc. BEDE. Not even meat offered to idols, so far as it is food, so far as it is a creature of God, but the invocation of demons makes it unclean. Hence: You cannot drink the chalice of the Lord and the chalice of devils (1 Cor. 10). The Jews boast of being a part of God, and call common those foods which all men use, such as oysters, hares, and such animals, which do not part the hoof, nor chew the cud, nor, among fish, have scales.
7.18: 7.18 And are you also without understanding? They are rebuked because they take for mystical what is plain of itself. From this we note that he is a faulty hearer who wishes to understand obscurely what is said plainly, or plainly what is said obscurely.
7.19: 7.19 And goes out into the privy. BEDE. Hence certain heretics cavil that the Lord, ignorant of natural science, thinks that all foods, etc., up to through hidden passages (which the Greeks call pores) it passes down to the lower parts and goes out into the privy. AUGUSTINE. Some things act in such a way that they both change and are changed, as food itself, losing its appearance, is turned into our body, and we, refreshed, are changed into strength.
7.21: 7.21 From within, out of the heart of men. BEDE. The principal seat of the soul is not, according to Plato, in the brain, but, according to Christ, in the heart. They are also rebuked, etc., up to so that if he sees us often gaze at a beautiful woman, he understands that we love her.
7.24: 7.24 And rising from thence. Leaving the Scribes and Pharisees, his calumniators, he withdrew into the parts of Tyre and Sidon, to heal the Tyrians and Sidonians. No man. BEDE. Although he could not be hidden, what he wished did not come to pass. But the example, etc., up to that he might free the daughter of the Syrophenician woman from the demon, and by the faith of a Gentile woman rebuke the unbelief of the Scribes and Pharisees.
7.25: 7.25 For a woman. Mark says that the Lord was in a house when the woman came to him. Matthew says that she cries after us (Matt. 15). By this he hints that she sent up her prayers after him as he walked. So the woman came to him in the house, but because Matthew says: He answered her not a word, he gave us to understand that both were silent and entered in silence. And so the rest is woven together, in which they nowhere disagree. JEROME. The woman is our mother, the Roman Church. Her daughter, the demoniac western barbarism, whose faith made a sheep out of a dog. She seeks the crumbs of understanding; she does not desire the unbroken bread of the letter. BEDE. The Gentile woman, but coming to the Lord with faith, signifies the Church gathered from the Gentiles, who for her daughter, etc., up to those who leave the former dwellings of their unbelief and with pious devotion transfer themselves into the house of God, that is, the Church.
7.27: 7.27 Let the children first be filled. As if he said: It will come to pass that you Gentiles also obtain salvation; but first it is fitting that the Jews, who by the ancient election are named children of God, be refreshed with the heavenly bread, and so at last the food of life be served to the Gentiles. Of the children. BEDE. A wonderful reversal: for Israel was once the son, and we the dogs. According to the difference of faith the order of names is changed. Of them it is said: Many dogs have encompassed me (Ps. 21). Of us: Other sheep I have that are not of this fold (John 10).
7.28: 7.28 Of the crumbs. I am not worthy to receive whole foods; I am content with the leavings of the little dogs, so that thus I may come to the whole bread. BEDE. Of the crumbs, etc. The table is Scripture, hence: You have prepared a table before me, etc. (Ps. 22). The crumbs of the children, etc., up to so that they may rightly lift themselves in humility to hope for the heavenly rewards promised by the Lord in heaven.
7.29: 7.29 For this saying. BEDE. Here an example is given for catechizing and baptizing infants, because through the faith and confession of their parents little children in baptism are freed from the demon, who cannot yet of themselves understand or do anything good or evil.
7.31: 7.31 Of Tyre. JEROME. Tyre, meaning distress, signifies Judea, to which the Lord says: The bed is straitened, and the short cloak cannot cover both, so that it may transfer itself to other nations (Is. 18). Sidon. JEROME. Sidon, meaning hunting, a wild untamed beast, is our region or nation. Decapolis. BEDE. A region of ten cities beyond the Jordan to the east. As to what is said, He came to the sea of Galilee through the midst of the borders of Decapolis, it does not mean that he entered them, for he is not said to have sailed across the sea, but to have come to the sea, and to the place which faced the midst of the borders of Decapolis, lying far across the sea. JEROME. The Savior is led by the apostles to save the Gentiles, and teaches what he answered to the young man who asked: You know the commandments; do this and you shall live (Luke 18).
7.32: 7.32 One deaf and dumb. BEDE. One who opens neither his ears to hear the words of God nor his mouth to speak. It is necessary that those who have learned by long practice to hear and speak the word of God offer such persons to the Lord to be healed, so that the right hand of grace may save those whom human frailty cannot. JEROME. The human race, like one man consumed by various plagues in the first-formed man, is blinded while it sees, becomes deaf while it hears, has its nostrils blown while it smells, is struck dumb while it speaks, becomes maimed while it raises its hands, is bent over while it is raised up, becomes dropsical while it desires, lame while it walks, is covered with leprosy while it is being cleansed, is filled with a demon while it seeks divinity, dies by death while it boldly makes excuses. And they besought him. The prophets and patriarchs desired the Incarnation of the Lord.
7.33: 7.33 And taking him, etc. He who deserves to be healed is led apart from turbulent thoughts and disordered acts and unseemly speeches. The fingers put into the ears are the words of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: This is the finger of God (Ex. 8). And: The heavens are the works of your fingers (Ps. 8). He touched his tongue, etc. The spittle from the flesh of the Lord is divine wisdom, which looses the ignorance of the human race, so that it may say: I believe in God the Father almighty, etc. Apart. BEDE. The first way of salvation is to be led out of the crowd. The Lord leads the sick man out of the crowd when he, etc., up to he therefore spits and touches the tongue of the dumb man that he may be able to speak, when by the touch of his mercy he forms mouths long mute to utter words of wisdom.
7.34: 7.34 And looking up, etc. JEROME. He sighed. He taught us to groan and to lift the treasure of our heart toward heaven, which is purged by compunction of heart from the frivolous joy of the flesh, as it is said: I roared with the groaning of my heart; Lord, all my desire is before you, etc. And he said to him: Ephpheta, that is, Be opened. With the heart we believe unto justice (Rom. 10), etc. And immediately they were opened, etc. The ears were opened to hymns and canticles and psalms. The tongue is loosed to utter a good word, which neither threats nor words can restrain or forbid. Hence Paul: I am bound, but the word of God is not bound in me (2 Tim. 2).
7.35: 7.35 And he spoke right. BEDE. He alone speaks rightly, either confessing the Lord or preaching to others, to whom divine grace restores hearing so that he can listen to heavenly things and obey the commands. His tongue the Lord instructs to speak by the touch of wisdom, which is himself. Such a man can say: Lord, you will open my lips (Ps. 5), etc.
7.36: 7.36 And he charged them that they should tell no man. He taught that we are to glory not in miracles but in the cross and in humiliation. But the more he charged them, etc. A city seated on a mountain cannot be hid (Matt. 15): humility always precedes glory. Be opened. Properly to the ears. For the ears had to be opened for hearing, the tongue to be loosed so that he might speak. Hence it follows: Immediately they were opened, etc. But the more he charged them, etc. He who knows all things before they happen knew that they would preach the more, and by commanding this he wished to show the slothful how much more zealously and frequently [fervently] those ought to preach whom he bids to preach, when those who are forbidden could not keep silent.
8.2: 8.2 I have compassion on the multitude. Because he is a true man, he has pity and compassion with the feeling of human frailty. That he filled four thousand men with seven loaves and a few little fishes is a work of divine power, against the error of Eutyches. They have now been with me three days. Why they stayed three days Matthew tells thus (Matt. 15): And going up into a mountain, he sat there, and they came to him, etc. The crowd waits on the Lord three days for the healing of their sick, when the elect, bright with faith in the holy Trinity, earnestly plead to the Lord for the sins of themselves and of their own, that is, for the languors of the sinning soul. A great multitude waits on the Lord three days when a multitude of the faithful, turning away from their sins by penance, turn to the Lord in work, in speech and in thought. BEDE. By this miracle it is signified that we cannot pass otherwise safely through the way of the present age unless Christ refreshes us with the food of his word. This typically, etc., up to he himself refreshes the soul drawn away from the lowest delights with the bread of heaven, and by giving a pledge of spiritual food kindles the appetite for heavenly sweetness.
8.3: 8.3 If I shall send them away. Because converted sinners faint on the way of the present life if they are sent away in their own conscience without the food of teaching. From afar. Morally: He who, having experienced no carnal corruption, hastens to the service of God does not come from afar; he also who has been defiled by no impurity, no shameful deeds, but has experienced only marriage, he too does not come from afar. Others come after many shameful deeds, and therefore from afar.
8.5: 8.5 Seven. BEDE. It is the mystery of the New Testament, in which the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is more fully believed and given. Nor are the loaves of barley, like those five from which five thousand men were filled, lest, as in the law, the nourishment of the living soul be covered by bodily sacraments. For the very tenacious kernel of barley is covered by chaff. JEROME. The seven loaves are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. Four thousand: the year of the New Testament with its four seasons. The seven baskets are the seven first Churches. The fragments of the loaves are those of the mystical understanding of the first week. The blessed little fishes are the books of the New Testament, as the risen Lord asks for a piece of broiled fish, and offers to the disciples a fish laid on coals in the catch of fishes.
8.6: 8.6 On the ground. BEDE. At the refreshment with five loaves the crowd sat down upon the grass; but those to be refreshed with seven loaves are commanded to sit on the ground, because through the law of the flesh, etc., up to but here, with all carnal desire removed, the solidity of the mountain itself, with no grass between, holds the guests of the New Testament as the firmament of abiding hope.
8.7: 8.7 Little fishes. THE SAME. The saints of that time, through whom the same Scripture was composed, or whose faith, life and sufferings the Scripture itself contains; who, rescued from the waves of the world and consecrated by divine blessing, have provided us refreshment, lest we faint in the course of this world, by the example of their life and death.
8.8: 8.8 They did eat. THE SAME. There are many who, though they cannot leave all their things and attain the higher things of this world, yet hungering and thirsting after justice are filled, when by hearing the commands of God they come to eternal life. That which remained over. THE SAME. The higher precepts or exhortations and counsels which the general multitude of the faithful cannot reach, as here: If you will be perfect, go, sell all you have (Matt. 19), etc. Seven baskets. The seven baskets are those filled with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. For baskets are made of rush and palm leaves. The rush grows upon the waters; the palm crowns the victor. The saints also, lest they dry up from the moisture of eternity, place themselves in the very fountain of life, and await the palm of eternal reward.
8.10: 8.10 And immediately. In place of this we have in Matthew: He went up into the boat and came into the coasts of Magedan. But there is no doubt that it is the same place under both names. For very many manuscripts have Magedan in Mark also.
8.11: 8.11 Seeking, etc. As if what they had seen were not signs. But what they seek by this is specified: from heaven, either fire from on high in the manner of Elijah, or, like Samuel, thunders to roar in summer time, or lightnings or rains, as if those who cavilled at things they had seen with their eyes, touched with their hands, and felt to their benefit could not cavil at these also. Or signs from heaven, such as manna, so that he who with a few loaves filled many thousands of men might now, like Moses, with manna sent from heaven refresh all the people everywhere. Hence John says that after the eating of the loaves the crowds asked: What work do you? Our fathers did eat manna in the desert (John 6), etc.
8.12: 8.12 If a sign shall be given. AUGUSTINE, On the Harmony of the Evangelists. In Mark he says it is written thus: and a sign shall not be given to it. BEDE. To this generation, that is, of those who tempt God and contradict his words, no sign shall be given from heaven, which those tempting, etc., up to at the laying on of the apostles' hands he poured out the grace of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon very many believers.
8.13: 8.13 He went up into the ship. THE SAME. Having just filled the seven baskets, they immediately went up into the boat and came into the coasts of Magedan, and there, as they sailed, they were told to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. But Scripture says that they forgot to take bread, which shows that they had little care for the flesh, being intent on the presence of the Lord.
8.17: 8.17 Why do you reason. BEDE. Taking the occasion, he teaches what the five loaves and the seven, and the few little fishes, and the five thousand men or four thousand signify. For if the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod signifies perverse traditions and heretical teachings, why do the foods by which the people of God was nourished not signify true and whole doctrine?
8.23: 8.23 And spitting. THE SAME. The spittle proceeds from within, from the head of the Lord. The hands are the members of the body placed outwardly. Spitting therefore on the eyes of the blind man, he lays his hands on him that he may see: because he wiped away the blindness of the human race both by the invisible gifts of divine mercy and by the sacraments shown outwardly of the humanity he assumed. He who could cure him wholly at once with one word, cures him gradually, to show the greatness of human blindness, how scarcely and as if by steps it returns to the light, and to point out to us his grace, by which the several increments of perfection help us.
8.24: 8.24 I see men, etc. JEROME. He esteems all men his superiors, judging himself unworthy: as David calls himself a man, but a dead dog and one flea. But first, etc., up to to him the Lord, by the second laying on of hands, restores the light of seeing all things clearly: namely what is to be believed, how to live, what rewards are to be hoped for.
8.25: 8.25 After that again, etc. JEROME. That he might see all things clearly, that is, understand invisible things through visible works, and with the eye of a clean heart contemplate what the eye has not seen, and the clear state of his soul after the rust of sin. For blessed are the clean of heart, for they shall see God (Matt. 5).
8.26: 8.26 And he sent him. JEROME. That he might see in himself what he had not seen before. For a man despairing of salvation does not think that he can altogether do what, once enlightened, he can accomplish through hope. Mystically: the Lord admonishes all who are enlightened by the knowledge of the truth to return to the heart, and weigh with anxious mind how much has been given them, and respond to the benefits of God with worthy action. Tell nobody. BEDE. That he bids him keep silent about the healing is an example for his own, that if they do wonderful things they should not seek favor, but be content to please the divine eyes.
8.27: 8.27 Whom do men say that I am? He fittingly asks first the opinion of men, lest their confession seem weakened by the opinion of the crowd rather than by recognition of the truth, lest, like Herod, they be thought to waver about what they had heard. Hence he says to Peter, according to Matthew: Flesh and blood has not revealed it to you (Matt. 16), that is, the teaching of men. Men. Fittingly those who, in the manner of men, hold diverse opinions about the Lord are called men. For those who with a pious mind know the truth of his power deserve to be called not men but gods. Hence he says to them: But you, etc. As if he said: They, men, think human things; but you, gods, whom do you say that I am?
8.29: 8.29 You are the Christ. BEDE. He embraces all things who expresses both the nature and the name, in which is the sum of the virtues. Paul says, etc., up to yet it is not permitted to be ignorant of the faith concerning his generation.
8.30: 8.30 And he strictly charged them. BEDE. He did not wish to be proclaimed before the passion and resurrection, because when the mystery of his blood was completed he says to the apostles more fittingly: Going, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 18). Because it would not have profited to proclaim publicly one whom they were about to see scourged and crucified, suffering many things.
8.31: 8.31 That the Son of man must, etc. JEROME. Like a skilled pilot who, foreseeing the storm in the calm, wants his sailors to be prepared. As elsewhere: If any man will come after me, let him deny himself (Matt. 16), etc.
8.32: 8.32 And Peter taking him. BEDE. Saying with the feeling of one who loves: Far be it from you, Lord. Or, as it reads better in the Greek: Be merciful to yourself, etc., up to and takes him to himself in affection, or leads him apart, so that he may not seem to rebuke the Master in the presence of the others.
8.33: 8.33 Go behind me. THE SAME. Many think that it is not Peter but the adversary spirit that was corrected, at whose suggestion the Apostle said this: But to me the error of the Apostle, coming from an affection of piety, will never seem an incentive of the devil. To the devil it is said: Go behind me, Satan. To Peter: Go behind me, etc., that is, follow my opinion. The things that are of God, etc. It is my will and the Father's that I die for the salvation of men: you do not wish the grain of wheat to fall into the ground that it may bring forth much fruit.
8.34: 8.34 If any man will, etc. BEDE. After he showed the mystery of his passion and resurrection, he exhorts all to imitate the example of the passion, and promises salvation of souls to all. But to the more perfect he disclosed how much he would suffer and that he would rise from the dead, giving a rule for preaching, namely that each be taught according to his own measure, and that higher things not be entrusted to the weak. Let him deny. He cannot lay hold of what is beyond himself if he does not know how to put to death what he is. Unless a man fail from himself, he does not draw near to God, who is above him. Take up his cross. Either by mortifying the body through abstinence, or the soul through compassion. Of the body Paul says: I chastise my body and bring it into subjection (2 Cor. 9), etc. The same of compassion of soul: Who is weak, and I am not weak? (2 Cor. 11).
8.38: 8.38 For he. BEDE. The Church signifies two times, one of persecution, when the soul is to be laid down; another of peace, when earthly desires are to be broken. For he who me, etc. Because many conquer avarice and despise passing things, but, hindered by shame, do not express in speech the right faith they have. He adds: For he who me, etc.
8.39: 8.39 Amen I say. BEDE. Since he was speaking of the future life, it was necessary to promise this of the life of penitence, that the disciples, still unlearned, might be strengthened by this consolation, as it is said of the Jewish people: He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labors of the people, that they might keep his justifications and seek after his law (Ps. 104). The kingdom of God, etc. That is, the Church raised up against the glory of this world. Or the future blessedness in the heavens which they saw on the mountain. This was done by pious foresight, so that eternal joy, though tasted beforehand for a brief moment, might more strongly encourage them to bear adversities.
9.1: 9.1 And after six days, etc. JEROME. After the threat of the cross the glory of the resurrection is shown, hence it follows: And after six days, etc. So that those who had seen with their own eyes the glory of the future resurrection would not fear the reproaches of the cross. BEDE. And after six days. Luke: And it came to pass about eight days after these words, etc., up to lest in the eighth, the time of recompense, we be rebuked by an angry judge. Into a high mountain. Into a mountain to pray, etc., up to then they will deserve to rejoice in his eternal vision. Transfigured. He did not lose the true substance of the flesh, but showed the glory of his future resurrection, or of ours. He will appear such to all the elect after the judgment; at the judgment, in the form of a servant to both good and bad, so that the wicked cannot recognize as judge him whom they scorned, whom the Jews denied, whom the soldiers crucified, whom Pilate and Herod judged.
9.2: 9.2 And his garments. The garments of the Lord are the saints. Hence: As many of you as have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ (Gal. 3). These seemed despised while the Lord remained in the world, but when he sought the mountain they shone with a new whiteness. For now we are the sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. When he shall appear, we shall be like to him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Hence it is added.
9.3: 9.3 And there appeared, etc. Moses, a saint who died, and Elijah, caught up alive into heaven, seen in majesty with the Lord (as Luke says), signify the future glory in him of all the saints, who at the time of the judgment will be found either alive in the flesh or dead. Elijah with. BEDE. The lawgiver and the foremost of the prophets appear: they speak with the Lord while he lives in the flesh, showing that he is the one whom the law and the prophets promised; not in the lowest place but on the mountain with him, because those who pass beyond earthly desires in mind perceive the majesty of holy Scripture, which was fulfilled in the Lord, being unfolded.
9.4: 9.4 Rabbi. Although stupefied, etc., up to having one tabernacle, that is, the Church of God. It is good. How much better, then, to take part in the choirs of the saints and enjoy the vision of the Godhead, if the transfigured humanity of Christ and the fellowship of two shown for a moment delights so.
9.6: 9.6 A cloud overshadowing. Hence, because he asked for a material tabernacle, he received the shade of a cloud, that he may learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be sheltered not by the covering of houses but by the Holy Spirit. This is. As if he said: This is truly he whom this Moses promised you, etc., up to and it will be illumined by grace itself and protected forever.
9.7: 9.7 And immediately. BEDE. When the voice came over the Son of man, he himself alone was found. Because when he has manifested himself to the elect, God will be all in all: indeed he with his own will shine as one Christ in all things, that is, the head with the body, hence: No man ascends into heaven but he that descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven (John 3).
9.8: 9.8 He charged them. He does not wish the glory of the future kingdom and triumph which he had shown on the mountain to be proclaimed publicly, lest it be both incredible because of its greatness, and lest, after so great a glory, the cross that followed should become a scandal to unlearned minds.
9.9: 9.9 They kept the word. JEROME. That is, when death shall be swallowed up in victory, former things will not be remembered, when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughter of Sion, taking away every tear from the eyes of the saints.
9.10: 9.10 What should this mean? The scribes hand down, according to Malachi, that Elijah will come before the coming of the Savior, and will turn the hearts of the fathers to their fathers, and restore all things to their ancient state. The disciples therefore reckon that this glory is the coming, which they had seen on the mountain, and say: If you have already come in glory, why does your forerunner not appear? especially since they see that Elijah has departed.
9.11: 9.11 Shall restore, etc. Namely he will turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to the fathers. For he will restore to death what he owes and has put off by living long, hence he adds: How it is written. As if he said: As the prophets in many ways wrote of the passion of Christ, so also Elijah is to suffer many things. He will therefore restore all things. First, the hearts of the men of that time to believe in Christ and to resist Antichrist. Then he will lay down his life for Christ.
9.13: 9.13 A great multitude. JEROME. There is no rest under the sun: envy always kills the little ones, lightnings strike the great mountains; some come to the Church learning with faith, others envying with pride. Disputing. BEDE. What they dispute the Evangelist does not say, but it can be understood that a question had been raised about why the disciples could not free the demoniac who was in the midst: for this can be gathered from what follows.
9.15: 9.15 And he asked. THE SAME. Note that the places agree with the matters. On the mountain he prays, is transformed, opens to the disciples the secrets of his majesty; below, he is received by the crowd, and is assailed by the weeping of the wretched. Above, he unlocks to the disciples the mysteries of the kingdom; below, he rebukes the crowds for the sins of unbelief. Above, he opens the voice of the Father to those who could hear; below, he casts out evil spirits. Now, according to the quality of their merits, he does not cease to ascend for some and to descend for others. And he asked. JEROME. He knows and asks, that confession may bring forth salvation, and the murmur of our heart be loosed in words first, as it is said: Tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified.
9.17: 9.17 And I spoke to your disciples. He secretly turns the blame on the disciples, since often the cure is hindered not by the fault of those who cure but of those to be cured.
9.18: 9.18 O unbelieving generation. He is angry not with the man but with the vice. He does not say this from weariness of feeling, but as a physician to a sick man who acts against the instructions. And through one man he accuses the Jews of unbelief.
9.19: 9.19 Immediately the spirit. Because when after sin we wish to be converted to the Lord, we are the more assailed by the devil, either to shake out the virtue or to avenge his own expulsion.
9.20: 9.20 From infancy. JEROME. It signifies the Gentile people, among whom the worship of idols grew up from birth, so that they foolishly sacrificed their sons to demons, hence it follows:
9.21: 9.21 And oftentimes, etc. For some venerated fire, others water. Help. JEROME. Our credulity, like a tongue with a beak, is weak unless it leans on the help of God. Faith with tears receives the desired prayers, as it is: Be it done to you according to your faith (Matt. 15).
9.25: 9.25 Tearing him, etc. JEROME. The devil tears those who approach salvation, which is his favorite food, whom he desires to draw into his belly through terrors and losses, as Job: Made, etc. ISIDORE, RABANUS, etc. For to the healed it is said: For you are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God (Col. 3). Hence the sickness of Christians is not death, but the likeness of death.
9.28: 9.28 This kind. JEROME. Folly belongs to the luxury of the flesh and is healed by fasting. Anger and sloth are driven out by prayer. The medicine proper to each wound is to be applied to it. What heals the heel does not heal the eye; the passions of the body are healed by fasting, the plagues of the mind by prayer.
9.30: 9.30 They shall kill him, etc. He mixes sad things with prosperous, so that when they come they may not be borne by unprepared minds. If it saddens them that he is to be killed, it ought to gladden them that on the third day he will rise again.
9.31: 9.31 They knew not. Not so much from slowness of understanding as from love, because they knew he was the true God, they could not believe he would die. And because they were accustomed to hear him speak in figures, shrinking from his death, they thought he spoke figuratively in these things also.
9.32: 9.32 Capharnaum. JEROME. Village of consolation: it suits the aforesaid saying: Killed, he will rise on the third day (John 12). The grain of wheat dies that it may be gathered the more manifold: if it does not die, it remains alone. What was it, etc., on the way. On the way they were discussing the primacy: the discussion is like the place. For primacy is entered by force, so it is abandoned, and while it is held it slips away: and it is uncertain in which dwelling, that is, on which day, it ends; hence he says: He who will be first, etc.
9.33: 9.33 They disputed among themselves. BEDE. This dispute seems to have arisen from the fact that they had seen Peter and James and John led apart to the mountain, and some secret believed to have been entrusted to them there, and also that to Peter, as Matthew says, the keys of the kingdom of heaven had been promised, and the Church to be built upon the rock of faith, from which he himself had received his name. They therefore thought that either those three were set over the others, or Peter over all.
9.34: 9.34 And sitting down, etc. They, while walking, disputed about the primacy, and he, sitting, teaches humility. For rulers labor, the humble rest. He wishes to heal the desire for glory by humility, and admonishes first by a simple command, then by the example of childlike innocence.
9.35: 9.35 Embracing. It signifies that the humble are worthy of his embrace, who can rightly glory and say: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me (Cant. 2).
9.36: 9.36 Whoever one. Either simply he shows that the poor of Christ are to be received, for his honor, by those who wish to be greater; or he urges that they be little children in malice, so as to be simple like little children. And whoever. Because he taught that he is received in the children, as the head in the members, lest it be thought that he was only what he seemed, he added: And whoever shall receive me, etc.
9.37: 9.37 John answered him. Because he had said: Whoever receives one such child receives me, John understands that they do not receive in his name those who do not walk sincerely; hence he says: Master, we saw one. As if he said: This one ought not to be received in your name. And we forbade him. He thought that he who does not use the office should be excluded from the benefit; but we are taught that no one is to be kept from the good which he has in part, but rather to be urged on to what he does not have: hence: Do not forbid him.
9.38: 9.38 Do not forbid. BEDE. Hence the Apostle: But whether by occasion or by truth, Christ be preached, etc., up to we ought to detest and forbid.
9.41: 9.41 And whoever shall scandalize. Although this is general, it can yet, following the sequence of the discourse, be said against the apostles, who disputed about primacy and could by their example destroy those whom they called to the faith. BEDE. Note that in our good work the scandal of our neighbor is sometimes to be avoided, sometimes to be counted as nothing: so far as we can without sin, we ought to avoid the scandal of our neighbors. But if scandal is taken on account of the truth, it is more useful that the scandal arise than that the truth be abandoned. A millstone. JEROME. According to the custom of the province, etc., up to the punishment of hell would torment him in some way more tolerably.
9.42: 9.42 And if he shall scandalize. Since above he taught that we should not scandalize those who believe in him, he admonishes how much we ought to beware of those who scandalize. In Greek, an offense, or a ruin, or a striking of the foot. Or, as others say, a stumbling-stone. He therefore scandalizes his brother who by word or deed gives him occasion of ruin. Your hand. A friend, whose help and counsel we need daily. But if he wishes to harm in the cause of the soul, he is to be shut out from our company, lest, if we wish to have part in this life with one who is lost, we perish together with him. Than having two hands. JEROME. The two hands are the two kinds of primacy, humility and pride. Cut off pride, keep the humble primacy.
9.43: 9.43 Where the worm. BEDE. The stench of worms comes from the corruption of flesh and blood, and therefore fresh flesh is seasoned with salt, so that, the bloody moisture being dried up, a worm cannot be. Flesh and blood therefore breed worms, because carnal delight, which the seasoning of continence does not resist, begets eternal punishment for the lustful. We ought therefore to chasten the body with the salt of continence, and the mind with the seasoning of wisdom, from the stain of error and vices.
9.48: 9.48 For every one shall be salted with fire. Because he made mention of fire and worm a third time, he shows how we can avoid both. For every one shall be salted with fire, it is wonderfully said: for what is salted with salt, salt keeps from the putrefaction of the worm. But what is by fire, that is, in fire, the sprinkled salt also consumes the flesh. These things were done according to the law in the victims which were burned on the altar, where it was commanded that salt be offered in every victim and sacrifice. Every victim shall be salted with salt. For he is truly the Lord's victim who, body and soul, etc., up to to deny those beloved and near to us. Every victim shall be salted with salt. JEROME. The victim is the human race, which here is salted with the salt of wisdom or reason, while the corruption of blood, the guard against putrefaction, and the mother of worms is consumed here, and afterward will be examined by the fire of purgatory.
9.49: 9.49 But if the salt, etc. That is, if anyone, once refreshed by the seasonings of truth, returns to apostasy, by what other teacher is he corrected, who spurns the wisdom he tasted, either frightened by adversity or enticed by prosperity? Hence: Who will pity an enchanter struck by a serpent? (Ecclus. 12). In this Judas and his companions are believed to be signified, who, corrupted by love of money, did not hesitate to lose the apostleship and to betray the Lord. But because there are many whom greater knowledge, while it lifts them up, separates from the company of others, and the more they know, the more they lose the virtue of concord, he adds: Have salt in you, and have peace. BEDE. To have salt without peace is not a gift of virtue but a proof of damnation. For the better anyone knows, the worse he offends.
10.1: 10.1 And rising up from thence. Up to this point he told what he did and taught in Galilee: from here he narrates what he did, taught and suffered in Judea. And first what was beyond the Jordan to the east; then what was on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho, and Bethany, and Jerusalem. For although the whole province of the Jews is called Judea generally, to distinguish it from other nations, yet more specially the southern region is called Judea, to distinguish it from Galilee, Decapolis, and the other regions in the same province.
10.2: 10.2 The Pharisees asked. There is a great distance between the crowds and the Pharisees. The crowds assemble to be taught and the sick to be cured, as Matthew plainly says: The Pharisees to deceive by tempting. For devotion of piety brings the former: the goad of envy the latter. If it is lawful for a man. BEDE. He tempted with a horned syllogism, etc., up to but was conceded by the necessity of sinners.
10.5: 10.5 For the hardness of your heart. THE SAME. Is God contrary to himself, etc., up to that the bond of marriage should continue through hatreds and murders.
10.8: 10.8 And they shall be, etc. The reward of marriage is that of two there be made one flesh. Chastity joined to the spirit becomes one spirit.
10.9: 10.9 Let not man put asunder. By desire of a second wife. God puts asunder: who joins, when by the consent of both, for the service of God (because the time is short), they have wives as if they had none.
10.10: 10.10 And in the house, etc. JEROME. The disciples did not ask first, etc., up to that bread may strengthen the heart of man, as it is: If any man will come after me (Luke 9), etc.
10.11: 10.11 Whoever shall put away. BEDE. Matthew more fully: Whoever shall put away his wife, except for fornication, and shall marry another, commits adultery (Matt. 5). There is therefore only one carnal cause, fornication; one spiritual, the fear of God, for a wife to be put away, as many are read to have done for the sake of religion. But there is no cause prescribed by the law of God for another to be taken while she who was left is alive.
10.13: 10.13 But the disciples rebuked those who brought them. Not that they were unwilling for them to be blessed by the hand and voice of the Savior, but, not yet having full faith, they thought he would be wearied, in the manner of men, by the importunity of those offering them.
10.14: 10.14 For of such is the kingdom of God. Of such he says significantly, not of these. As if he said: Character reigns, not age. The kingdom of heaven is promised to those who have like simplicity and innocence, to whom fits that saying of the Apostle: Do not become children in sense, but in malice be children (1 Cor. 14).
10.15: 10.15 Whoever shall not receive the kingdom. He who does not persist in anger, when hurt does not remember it, seeing a beautiful woman does not lust, does not have one thing in his mouth and another in his heart. As if he said: If you are not such, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of God. That is, we are commanded to receive the doctrine of the Gospel as little children, that is, as a little child does not contradict its teachers, does not compose arguments against them, but receives faithfully, obeys with fear and is quiet: so we also ought to receive the words of the Lord by obeying simply and without any contradiction.
10.17: 10.17 Running up, and kneeling. BEDE. He had heard, I believe, from the Lord that only those who wish to be like little children are worthy of entrance into the heavenly kingdom, and so he desires to be more certain, not by parables but plainly: by what merits of works he may obtain eternal life.
10.18: 10.18 Why do you call me. THE SAME. Because he had called him good Master, etc., up to but he testifies that apart from God there is no good.
10.19: 10.19 Do not commit adultery. THE SAME. This is the chastity of childlike innocence, which is set before us to imitate, if we wish to enter the kingdom of God. It should surely be noted that the justice of the law, kept in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but also eternal life.
10.20: 10.20 Master. THE SAME. He is not to be thought of as tempting, by his wish, etc., up to hence he adds: Go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor (Matt. 5), etc.
10.21: 10.21 And come, follow me. THE SAME. As if he said: After despising riches, imitate the Savior, that is, leave evil things and do good. A purse is more easily despised than concupiscence or pleasure.
10.23: 10.23 How hard. THE SAME. Those who devote themselves to multiplying riches, etc., up to may enter the kingdom of God.
10.25: 10.25 It is easier for a camel. How then did Matthew and Zacchaeus and Joseph in the Gospel, and in the Old Testament very many rich men, enter? Perhaps because they held riches as nothing or had learned to despise them wholly; hence David: I am alone and poor (Ps. 24). And the same: If riches abound, set not your heart upon them (ibid. 61). He did not say, do not receive them.
10.26: 10.26 And who then can be saved? Since the poor are more numerous than the rich, they would not have said this unless they understood, in the number of the rich, all who wished to obtain riches.
10.27: 10.27 With God. Who can turn a man from desire of earthly things to the love of eternal things, and make the proud humble.
10.28: 10.28 Behold, we have left all things. Great confidence: he was a fisherman, he was not rich, he sought his living by hand and craft, and yet he says confidently: Behold, we have left all things. And have followed you. Because it is not enough to leave in this way, he adds what is perfect, and have followed you. As if he said: We have done what you commanded: what reward then will you give?
10.30: 10.30 A hundredfold. BEDE. On this occasion some teach the Jewish fable of a thousand years after the resurrection of the just, etc., up to of the heavenly homeland, which is signified by the right hand, all the elect alike enjoy it with the truest love.
10.31: 10.31 But many. Because many begin but do not complete, a terrible sentence is added: But many, etc. The thief on the cross, a confessor on the same day on which he was crucified for his sins, by the grace of faith rejoices with Christ in paradise. We also see daily many laymen excel more in merits of life, and others, fervent in spiritual zeal from their first age, grow numb at last in idleness.
10.32: 10.32 And they were amazed. Namely because they remembered that he had foretold that he would suffer many things from the chief priests and scribes, and be put to death. They feared therefore that either they themselves would be killed with him, or that he, in whose life and teaching they rejoiced, would be killed. And taking. BEDE. Foreseeing that the minds of the disciples would be troubled by his passion, etc., up to he goes to the place of death as one undaunted.
10.35: 10.35 And there come. Having heard of the resurrection, forgetful of the second coming, they think he will reign in the manner of men. Matthew says the mother made the request, but Mark says they did, wishing to disclose the desire of those on whose counsel the mother asked.
10.38: 10.38 Or the baptism. The same as the chalice. Hence elsewhere he says of his passion: I have a baptism wherewith I am to be baptized: and how am I straitened until it be accomplished.
10.39: 10.39 The chalice indeed. BEDE. James is beheaded by Herod, John is cast into a cask of boiling oil. From there the athlete of Christ advanced to the crown of martyrdom, and was immediately banished to Patmos. Thus he did not lack the spirit of martyrdom, and drank the chalice of confession which the three children drank in the furnace, though the persecutor did not shed his blood.
10.40: 10.40 But to sit. As if to say: Do you want me to grant you this? But the kingdom of heaven belongs not to the giver but to the receiver. For there is no respect of persons with God (Acts 10), but whoever is worthy will receive what is prepared not for the person but for the life. For you. They are still proud, as if he said: If you want to receive, do not be what you are: it is prepared for others, and you be others, and it is prepared for you, which is, you who now want to be exalted must first be humbled.
10.41: 10.41 They were moved with indignation. Not about the mother, but about the sons, who, ignorant of their own measure, burned with immoderate desire.
10.42: 10.42 But Jesus calling them. The humble Master, kind and gentle, neither rebukes the two for immoderate desire nor reproaches the ten for indignation and envy, but teaches that he is greater who is less, and he is lord who is servant. In vain, therefore, either these sigh for greater things or those grieve over their desire, since not power but humility leads to the summit of the virtues. Finally he sets an example for his own, so that if they made light of his words they might be ashamed before his works. For the Son of man also, etc.
10.46: 10.46 And they come to Jericho. JEROME. Jericho means moon, or anathema, which suits one approaching his passion. The waning of Christ's flesh is the preparation of the heavenly Jerusalem, hence, leaving Jericho, they approach Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace. And as he went out. BEDE. Because as the Lord ascended to the heavens and the faithful followed, etc., up to and he scattered them into the world for the enlightenment of all peoples. Bartimaeus the blind man. JEROME. The blindness of the Jews, which will be enlightened at the end at the coming of Elijah and Enoch.
10.47: 10.47 Who when he heard. The people of the Gentiles, having heard the fame of Christ, of which it sought to become a partaker, many contradicted, first the Jews, afterward the Gentiles also, that the world, about to be enlightened and healed, should not call on Christ; yet the fury of the opponents could not hinder those predestined to eternal life. Son of David. JEROME. Through the merits of the patriarchs the Jewish people is enlightened, to whom God is present, merciful and compassionate, enlightening the blind and raising up the crushed.
10.48: 10.48 But he cried much more. As the war of the vices grows heavier, hands must be lifted with a cry to the stone of help, that is, to Jesus. JEROME. A fitting order of salvation, etc., up to the apostles considering the heights.
10.49: 10.49 And they call the blind man. BEDE. Allegorically, the Lord calls the blind man who cries out when he entrusts the word of faith, through holy preachers, to the people of the Gentiles who desire the knowledge of truth. Those calling the blind man command him to be of good heart and rise, and come to him, when by preaching they bid him have hope of salvation, rise from the torpor of vices, and gird himself for the pursuit of the virtues by which he may deserve to be enlightened, as if to say: Come to him and be enlightened (Ps. 33). And: Arise, you that sleep (Eph. 5), etc.
10.50: 10.50 Who casting off his garment. That is, having cast off the cares of the world, with unencumbered step of mind he hastens to the giver of light. Leaping up. He rewards ready will with the fulfillment of desire, hence: Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you shall receive.
10.51: 10.51 Rabboni, that I may see. He does not seek gold but light. For a blind man can have riches, but does not see what he has. By his example let us seek not false riches but the light which we can see with the angels alone, to which faith is the way. Hence to the enlightened blind man it is said: Go, your faith has made you whole.
10.52: 10.52 He saw and followed. BEDE. He sees and follows who works what he understands well. To follow is to imitate. Hence: If any man serve me, let him follow me (John 12). In the way. Let us consider by what way he walks, and follow through humility, through labors. The way that says: I am the way, the truth and the life (John 14). This is the narrow way that leads to the steep places, to Jerusalem and Bethany at the Mount of Olives, which is the mountain of light and consolation.
11.1: 11.1 Bethany. BEDE. Bethany is a village or city on the side of Mount Olivet, etc., up to two on account of the knowledge of truth and the cleanness of work. Two of his disciples. JEROME. They are called two by two, sent two by two, etc., up to between the two cherubim they know the Lord, singing psalms in spirit and mind.
11.2: 11.2 And immediately. BEDE. The preachers entering the world found the people of the nations, etc., up to but he who is clean and holy belongs to God alone.
11.4: 11.4 The colt tied. JEROME. The colt tied and untamed, which they loose and tame, is the Gentile people. Before the door of faith, with the chains of its sins, it stands at the crossroads: in freedom of choice it hesitates between death and life.
11.6: 11.6 And they let them go. BEDE. Those who objected to the loosing, etc., up to that they cover themselves worthily with Christ as rider.
11.7: 11.7 And he sat. JEROME. He began to reign so that sin may not reign in the mortal or wanton flesh, but justice and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
11.8: 11.8 And many spread. Because many martyrs, stripping themselves of the garment of their own flesh, prepare the way with their blood for the simpler, that they may advance unhurt to the heavenly city to which Jesus leads. JEROME. Many, etc. The feet are the extremities, which the Apostle appointed to be joined on, which, though they are not the back on which the Lord sat, are nevertheless instructed with the soldiers by John. And others. THE SAME. The just shall flourish like the palm, narrow in the roots, broad in flowers and fruits: for they are the good odor of Christ, and they strew the way of the commandments of God with good report. BEDE. And others cut down leaves or branches from the trees, who in the teaching of truth extract words and sentences of the Fathers from their books. And these they lay in the way of God, for the soul of the hearer who comes, by humble preaching.
11.9: 11.9 And they that went before. The Jewish people went before, the Gentile followed. And because all who are or were faithful believed and believe in Christ, both those who go before and those who follow cry hosanna, which in Latin is Save us: for all the earlier ones also sought salvation from him.
11.10: 11.10 Blessed is he that comes. Since there is one faith, one hope of all. They awaited him and believed he would come, and we believe he has come. BEDE. By what is added, hosanna in the highest, which is salvation, it signifies that his coming is the salvation not only of men but of the whole world, joining earthly things to heavenly, that every knee should bow to him, of those in heaven, on earth and under the earth (Phil. 2). JEROME. This agrees with Gabriel, who says: He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High, etc., up to through the very word of entreaty.
11.11: 11.11 And he entered. THE SAME. Now as the passion draws near, he wishes to be in the place appointed for the passion before the ages, etc., up to he has already begun the sacrament of the blessed immolation. Into the temple. He gave us an example that wherever we come, we should first turn aside to the house of prayer if there be one, and when we have commended ourselves to God by zeal in prayer, withdraw to do the things for which we came. And having looked round about, etc. He did this not once but through all five days. By day he taught in the temple, and at night, going out, he stayed on the Mount of Olives, as Luke says. For by teaching he diligently devoted the office of correction to the unbelieving, and by staying with the faithful he graciously showed the grace of kindness. And when he had seen. BEDE. As he speaks through parables, so he acts, etc., up to by working miracles, and he found none: therefore he condemned it.
11.14: 11.14 No more. THE SAME. You also, if you do not wish to hear from Christ in the judgment, Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire, for I was hungry and you gave me not to eat (Matt. 25), take care not to be a barren tree, but rather offer to Christ, poor and hungry, the fruit of piety of which he is in need.
11.15: 11.15 He began to cast out. In the very thing he shows what he did by figure in the fig tree. For the fig tree did not sin if it had no fruit before its time, but the priests did. Them that sold. BEDE. That is, the things which those who came from afar bought from the natives to offer, etc., up to are always deprived of the priesthood.
11.16: 11.16 And he suffered not. He sends ahead an example of the future judgment, when he drives all the reprobate from the Church, and restrains them with an eternal scourge from entering it again to disturb it. But you have made it. For they were in the temple for this: either to persecute bodily those who did not give, or to kill spiritually those who did. The temple and house of God is the mind and conscience of the faithful, which in the injury of a neighbor brings forth perverse thoughts, as if thieves lodged in a den and killed those walking simply: and so the mind is no longer the house of God but a den of thieves.
11.20: 11.20 Dried up. BEDE. The fig tree was withered from the roots, to show that the impious nation was not to be rebuked for a time or in part by the incursions of foreigners and delivered through penance, as often happened, but struck with complete and eternal damnation. Otherwise: It was withered from the roots, to show that it was to be utterly forsaken not only by human favor outwardly but by divine favor within: for it lost both life in heaven and country on earth.
11.21: 11.21 And Peter remembering. Peter recognizes the withered tree and the root cut off, to which succeeds the most beautiful, fruitful olive called by the Lord. Hence it follows: Amen I say to you, etc.
11.23: 11.23 Whoever shall say. BEDE. Some are accustomed to say that our people had not yet full faith, etc., up to how much he groans that he has been driven out from the injury of the pious. JEROME. But this was done when the apostles said: Worthily we are transferred to the Gentiles, because you judge yourselves unworthy (Matt. 21). BEDE. The distinction of those who pray is to be noted, etc., up to if, however, they first forgive those who sin against them.
11.25: 11.25 And when you shall stand. JEROME. Mark, in his manner, comprises the seven verses of the Lord's Prayer in one prayer. For he to whom all things have been forgiven, what more will he ask, except that he persevere in what he has obtained?
11.28: 11.28 By what authority. They doubt about the power of God, and want it understood that what he does is the devil's.
11.29: 11.29 I will ask you. He could have refuted the calumny of the tempters by a plain answer: but he prudently asks, that they may be condemned either by their silence or by their answer.
11.31: 11.31 If we say. JEROME. They are darkened by the lamp of the world, hence it is said: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ: his enemies I will clothe with confusion (Ps. 131). Why then, etc. As if he said: He whom you confess to have had prophecy from heaven bore witness to me, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things.
11.32: 11.32 If we say. Whichever of these they answer: they see that they will fall into the snare, they fear stoning: but more, the confession of truth.
11.33: 11.33 Neither do I tell you. BEDE. The knowledge of truth is hidden from seekers for two reasons: when either he who seeks understands too little, or through hatred or contempt of the truth he is unworthy that it should be opened to him. For the one it is said: I have yet many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. For the other: Give not that which is holy to dogs.
12.1: 12.1 A pit, or winepress, or altar, or those winepresses from whose titles certain psalms are headed. Went into a far country. Giving free will to act, not by change of place, since God is everywhere and fills all things.
12.6: 12.6 They will reverence. He did not say this out of ignorance, because he knows all things, but God is always said to be in doubt so that free will may be reserved to man. BEDE. We ask Arius and Eunomius: behold, the Father is said to be ignorant, and he tempers his judgment, and, as far as in us lies, is said to have lied. Whatever they answer for the Father, let them understand the same for the Son, who says he does not know the day of the consummation.
12.7: 12.7 But the husbandmen. THE SAME. He proves that the princes of the Jews did not crucify Christ through ignorance, etc., up to and they strove to set above him their own justice which is of the law.
12.8: 12.8 And they cast him out. He marks their obstinacy: for they were unwilling to believe the preaching of the apostles even after the Lord had been crucified and raised, but cast him out like a worthless corpse: because, as far as in them lay, excluding him from their borders, they gave him to the Gentiles to be received. BEDE. Whoever of the faithful has the mystery of baptism, etc., up to will rejoice to crucify the Lord and hold him up to ridicule.
12.10: 12.10 The stone which they rejected. JEROME. The rejected stone, which became the corner, joining at the supper the lamb with the bread, ending the Old Testament and beginning the New, this presents marvels in our eyes.
12.13: 12.13 And they send to him. BEDE. They feared the crowd, and what they could not do by themselves, etc., up to and preferred to lose both the kingdom and everything rather than be tributaries.
12.14: 12.14 Master, we know. THE SAME. A flattering and fraudulent question provokes the respondent to fear God rather than Caesar, and to say that tribute ought not to be paid, so that the Herodians who hear may hold him as the author of sedition against the Romans.
12.15: 12.15 But he knowing their wickedness. Those who think the Savior's question to be ignorance and not dispensation, let them learn from this place that he could know whose image it was. But he asks, that he may answer their words fittingly. A penny. The denarius is a kind of coin reckoned as ten coins, and it bears the image of Caesar.
12.17: 12.17 Render therefore the things that are Caesar's. He did this himself: by paying tribute for himself and for Peter. And the things that are God's to God. This also he did, fulfilling the will of the Father. Otherwise: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, the impression of his image. And to God the things that are God's, the soul enlightened by the light of his countenance, hence: The light of your countenance is signed upon us (Ps. 4), etc.
12.18: 12.18 The Sadducees, etc. There were two heresies among the Jews, of the Pharisees and Sadducees. The Pharisees set before all the justice of traditions and observances (as they call them), hence they are called divided by the people. The Sadducees, that is, the just, denied the resurrection both of body and soul. The Sadducees, etc. BEDE. Those who deny the resurrection of bodies, or do not believe that souls in judgment do not perish with their bodies, rightly invent such a fable as would convict of folly those who assert the resurrection of bodies. Yet it could also at some time have happened among their people.
12.20: 12.20 There were therefore seven, etc. THE SAME. They set up the shamefulness of the fable in order to deny the resurrection. But mystically, the seven brothers who died without children fit all the reprobate: who throughout life (which revolves in seven days) are barren of good work, and when they die one by one, at last the worldly way of life itself also dies, that is, passes away, like a barren wife, whom they treated without fruit of good work. JEROME. The barren woman, leaving no seed from the seven brothers, etc., up to because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.
12.25: 12.25 They shall neither marry, nor, etc. BEDE. The Latin usage does not correspond to the Greek idiom: for women are properly said nubere (to marry), and men ducere (to lead a wife). But let us understand the simple meaning: neither shall men marry, nor women be married.
12.26: 12.26 I am the God, etc. BEDE. Though he could have produced many plainer testimonies about the resurrection, etc., up to which they did, good or evil, with their souls.
12.28: 12.28 He asked him. JEROME. What does this question mean, since all who are learned in the law know this? But the commandments are ordered differently in Exodus and Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For on these two breasts raised upon the bosom of the spouse our infancy is nourished. The first of all, etc. The greatest, which before all things we ought to place in the heart as the sole foundation of piety, that is, the knowledge and confession of divine unity with the carrying out of the divine work, which is perfected in the love of God and neighbor: this is the faith which works by charity.
12.32: 12.32 Well, Master. BEDE. The scribe shows in this answer that a grave question had long been debated among the scribes and Pharisees, etc., up to but no one without faith and love, in which opinion this scribe declares himself to have been.
12.34: 12.34 You are not far from the kingdom of God, etc. ISIDORE. Although he came to tempt: for ignorance is farther away than knowledge, as it is said to the Sadducees: You err, not knowing the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matt. 22). BEDE. Matthew says that he sought by tempting, etc., up to according to that: He that is hasty to give credit is light of heart, and shall be diminished (Ecclus. 19). And no man. Because they are confuted in words, they ask no more; but openly seizing him, they deliver him to the Roman power, hence it is clear that the poisons of envy can be overcome, but it is difficult for them to rest.
12.36: 12.36 Sit on my right hand. For in this he shows not the weakness of the Son but that one works in the other. For the Son also subjects enemies to the Father, and glorifies God the Father upon the earth.
12.38: 12.38 Beware. BEDE. Note that he does not forbid those who hold this office, etc., up to we be seduced by pretense, or be inflamed by emulation to the same.
12.40: 12.40 Who devour the houses of widows. As if they were advocates in the coming judgment, they do not hesitate to take money from the weak and from those troubled by the conscience of sins: whereas the hand stretched out to give, not gathered to receive, commends prayer to God: to which fits that saying: Let his prayer be turned to sin.
12.41: 12.41 The treasury. BEDE. In Greek, gaza; in Latin, to keep. Gaza, in Persian, means riches; the treasury is the place where riches are kept, and the chest, namely, in which the gifts of the people were collected for the uses of the temple. Hence in the book of Kings: Joiada the high priest took one chest, and opened a hole in the top of it (4 Kings 12), etc., and the porches in which they were kept. Hence: These words Jesus spoke in the treasury, teaching in the temple. He observed how. As he said that those who seek primacy and vainglory are to be avoided, and foretold a heavier judgment for those who pray with pretense, so also he distinguishes those who offer by just examination, to render to each according to heart and works, which he does today also in the Church. The rich. BEDE. The rich, the Jews puffed up with the justice of the law, etc., up to they furnish for all the works of the proud Jews.
12.42: 12.42 A poor widow. JEROME. This poor little woman signifies me and those like me, who give what I can and desire what I cannot explain to you. God desires not how much, but from how much. Everyone can offer a farthing. This is the cake of bread in Leviticus, which is ready will. A farthing, because it consists of three, thought, word and deed. A farthing. Calculators call a farthing the fourth part of anything, namely of place, time, money. Perhaps therefore here it signifies the fourth part of a shekel, that is, five obols.
12.44: 12.44 For all. BEDE. The Jew puts into the gifts from his abundance, etc., up to My God, his mercy shall prevent me (Ps. 58).
13.1: 13.1 And as he went out. BEDE. When the Lord leaves the temple, etc., up to was about to pay the penalty, and the buildings were to fall. Do you see these, etc. It was divinely arranged that, when the grace of the Gospel faith had been made known through the world, the temple itself with its ceremonies should be taken away: lest perhaps someone still a little child, and a suckling in the faith, if he saw those things made by the prophets and instituted by the Lord remain, admiring the worldly holy place, should gradually slip back to Judaism. The shadow is therefore taken away, and the truth declared through the world holds the palm. JEROME. He foretells the disaster of the last time, that is, the destruction of the temple with its people and its letter. Of which: There shall not be left a stone upon a stone (Luke 21): that is, the testimonies of the prophets upon those against whom the Jews twisted them, as in Ezra, in Zerubbabel, in the Maccabees.
13.3: 13.3 And as he sat, etc. BEDE. He remains quiet among the saints, while he abhors the madness of the proud. For the Mount of Olives signifies the fruitful height of the Church: that mountain produces not unfruitful trees but olive groves, by which light is nourished, rest is given to the weary, and weakness is loosed.
13.5: 13.5 And Jesus answering. THE SAME. From the time of the Lord's passion neither wars of enemies nor seditions of citizens ceased among the people of the Jews, who chose a seditious robber and rejected Christ the Savior; but the apostles are admonished that they not be frightened when these things come, and not leave Jerusalem and Judea, because the end is not yet. For the desolation of the province and the final destruction of the city and temple were put off to the fortieth year.
13.6: 13.6 For many shall come. As the destruction drew near, many came who falsely claimed to be Christs and that the time of liberty was now at hand. Many in the Church also, in the times of the apostles, among other things, threatened that the day of the Lord was at hand. Many came in the name of Christ as Antichrists, of whom the first was Simon Magus, to whom all in Samaria, from the least to the greatest, gave heed, saying: This man is the power of God, which is called great: because for a long time he had bewitched them with magical arts.
13.8: 13.8 For nation shall rise. BEDE. All these things before the last and bitterest sorrows, etc., up to who, fighting against one another, bring about the victory of the Church.
13.9: 13.9 But take heed. BEDE. Why all these things are brought upon them he says: Take heed, etc. For this is the one greatest cause of the destruction, that after the killing of the Lord they likewise vexed with impious cruelty the heralds and confessors of his name and faith.
13.10: 13.10 And unto all nations. THE SAME. Because the Lord knew that the hearts of the disciples would be saddened at the perdition of their nation, he consoles them in this way, that they may know that, the Jews being lost, they will have companions of the heavenly kingdom from the whole world. For as ecclesiastical histories testify, long before the destruction of Judea all the apostles were scattered to preach the Gospel through the whole world, except James the son of Zebedee, and James the brother of the Lord, who first shed their blood in Judea for the word of the Gospel.
13.14: 13.14 And when you shall see, etc. THE SAME. The abomination can be understood as either Antichrist, or the image of Caesar which Pilate set up in the temple, etc., up to always obeyed the empire of the Romans.
13.17: 13.17 And woe to them that are with child, etc. Because, burdened either by the weight of the womb or the burden of their children, they will not be able to flee. Hence in the book of Histories it is read that the wife of Jonathan, troubled by flight, received her son, who had slipped from her bosom, lame for life.
13.21: 13.21 And then if any man. BEDE. Some refer this to the Jewish captivity, when many, saying they were Christs, drew the deceived people after them. But there was no faithful man there whom God might exhort not to follow perverse masters. All, both besiegers and besieged, were hardened, alien from Christ, hence it is better understood of heretics, who, coming against the Church, falsely say they are Christs: of whom the first is Simon Magus; the last, Antichrist.
13.24: 13.24 But in those days, etc. THE SAME. The stars will be seen darkened in the judgment, etc., up to then shall be fulfilled what the same prophet says elsewhere: And the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days (Is. 3).
13.25: 13.25 Falling. From the light, when the seed of Abraham, to which the stars are likened, will almost fail. And the powers which, etc. BEDE. What wonder that men tremble, when at the sight of the judgment even the angelic powers tremble? Hence Job: The pillars of heaven tremble, and dread at his beck (Job 26). And what will the twig of the desert suffer, where the cedar of paradise is shaken? Shall be moved. JEROME. To the wrath of vengeance, when they shall be sent by the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power, who first came down like rain upon the fleece, in humility.
13.27: 13.27 From the four winds. From east and west, south and north, and not only from these, but from the top of the earth to the top of heaven, that is, from the extreme ends of the earth straight on to its last limits, where to those looking far off the circle of heaven seems to sit upon the earth.
13.28: 13.28 Now of the fig tree. As if he said: As when the fig tree has tender shoots and the bud bursts into flower, you understand the coming of summer and spring and the west wind; so when you see these things that are written, do not think that the end of the world is already here, but that they come as forerunners to show that it is near. BEDE. The fig tree is the Synagogue, which, because when the Lord came to it it had no fruit of justice, etc., up to and the summer of true light and peace. JEROME. The parable of the fig tree, that is, prophecy. The leaves that have sprouted are present words, and summer is the near day of judgment, in which every tree will make manifest what it had within, whether dry for burning, or green for planting in Eden with the tree of life, whose leaves are for the salvation of the nations, that is, the words by which it will be said: Come, ye blessed of my Father, etc.
13.31: 13.31 Heaven and earth shall pass away. The airy heaven, from which come the birds of the air and the clouds of heaven, hence Peter: But the heavens that now are, and the earth, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire (2 Pet. 3), teaching plainly that the heavens that are to perish by fire are other than those destroyed by water, that is, the empty and misty. For the water of the flood, which rose only fifteen cubits above the mountain tops, did not reach beyond the confines of air and ether. Ecclesiastes, ch. 1: One generation passes away, and another generation comes: but the earth stands for ever. So heaven and earth pass away according to their image, but remain for ever according to their essence.
13.32: 13.32 Neither the Son. For in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. They are hidden because it does not profit us to know, hence he says: It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has put in his own power (Acts 1). In this he shows that he knows, but that knowing is not expedient for the apostles, so that, always uncertain about the coming of the judge, they may live every day as if they were to be judged the next. The Son therefore knows for himself, but not for us, that we may always be anxious, hence: Take heed, watch, etc. HILARY. The Son and the Holy Spirit, because they are not from themselves, do not know of themselves about that day; but the Father, because he is from himself, knows from himself.
13.34: 13.34 And commanded the porter, etc. JEROME. That is, him who preaches. To whom it is said: If you do not declare to the wicked his iniquity, I will require his blood at your hand (Ezek. 3). Watch ye therefore. After setting forth the example of the father of the family, he says why he conceals the day of the consummation: watch ye therefore. He who sleeps sees not bodies but phantasms, and when he wakes he has nothing of what he had seen. So are those whom the love of the world seizes in life, and deserts after life.
13.36: 13.36 And what I say to you. We are commanded that not only the rulers of the Church but all watch, guarding the doors of the heart, lest the evil suggestion of the ancient enemy enter, lest the Lord find us sleeping, hence Paul: Watch, you just, and sin not.
14.1: 14.1 Now the Pasch was. JEROME. Pasch is interpreted passage, and phase, immolation, etc., up to and, armed with virtue, let us eat, saying: For Christ our Pasch is sacrificed (Matt. 26). BEDE. Pasch, which in Hebrew is phase, from passing, not from suffering, etc., up to it admonishes us to undertake the journey of the virtues. And the chief priests sought. JEROME. Iniquity went forth from the princes, who ought to have prepared the temple, and the vessels, and purified themselves according to the law for the eating of the lamb.
14.2: 14.2 Not on the festival day. THE SAME. They avoid the festival day, which is fitting for them: there is no feast for those who have lost life and mercy.
14.3: 14.3 And when he was in Bethany. THE SAME. The fawn of the harts always returns to its bed, that is, the Son obedient to the Father unto death: he asks obedience of us. For Simon is interpreted obedient. Of Simon the leper. Simon the leper signifies the unbelieving world first, and afterwards the believing. And as he sat at table, there came, etc. As he reclined, that is, humbled himself, so that the faith of the sinner might touch him: who ascends from the feet to the head, and from the head descends through faith, that is, from Christ to his members. A woman. BEDE. Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus whom the Lord raised, etc., up to as Matthew and Mark testify, poured holy oil. An alabaster box. Alabaster is white marble marked with various drops, and preserves ointments uncorrupted. Of spikenard. Pistic nard is said to be mixed, because it was compounded not only from the root but from the spikes and leaves, which is more precious. And breaking. JEROME. The house filled with the odor is heaven and earth. The broken alabaster is carnal desire, which is broken at the head: from whom the whole body is compacted. BEDE. The devotion of Mary signifies the faith and piety of the Church, etc., up to she venerates with pious preaching and devout obsequies.
14.4: 14.4 Now there were some. THE SAME. By synecdoche he put the plural for the singular, etc., up to and took care to disclose his habit of stealing for this reason. To what purpose is this waste? JEROME. The lost man found perdition in salvation, so that in the fruitful fig tree he found the snare of death.
14.5: 14.5 For it might have been sold. THE SAME. Under the pretext of avarice he speaks the mystery of faith, etc., up to let us divide the spoils in the evening.
14.6: 14.6 She has wrought a good work. THE SAME. He who believes in God, it is reckoned to him as a work of justice. For it is one thing to believe him, another to believe in him, that is, to cast oneself wholly into him.
14.7: 14.7 But me you have not always. BEDE. United by bodily presence and familiarity as now. Hence the Apostle: Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, but now we know him so no longer (2 Cor. 5). But spiritually he is always with us, hence: Behold I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the world. JEROME. It is to be understood thus: But me you will not always have in bodily presence, as before in companionship and familiarity.
14.8: 14.8 What she had. What you think is a waste of the ointment is the office of burial. No wonder if she gave me the good odor of faith, when I am about to pour out my blood for her.
14.9: 14.9 Amen I say to you. BEDE. Note in Christ the knowledge of things to come: he foreknows that after a few days they will suffer, and that his Gospel is to be preached in the whole world. It is to be noted that as Mary, in the whole world where the Church is spread, earned glory for the pious service she devoutly rendered to the Lord, so also Judas, who found fault with it, is defamed far and wide with the mark of unbelief. But the Lord rewards the good with pious praise, and is silent about the reproaches of the impious to come.
14.10: 14.10 One of the twelve. JEROME. One in number, not in merit, in name not in divinity, in body not in soul, hence the bridegroom to the bride: You have wounded my heart, my sister, with one of your eyes, and with one hair of your neck (Cant. 4). The eye and the hair are wisdom and power, since to Judas with the others it is said: To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God (Matt. 13).
